SCAM WARNING If anyone asks you for money or any kind of payment to help you publish, protect, restore, or undelete a Wikipedia article or draft page, it is a scam . Please report it to paid-en-wp wikipedia.org . Learn more about scams on Wikipedia . How to hide this warning This page in a nutshell: The topic of the article must be notable : it must have in-depth coverage in reliable sources that are independent of the topic. If you are connected to the topic, follow the Conflict of interest guidelines. Make sure there isn't already an article about the topic. The article you write must include citations to the sources you used. Use your own words to write the article; you must not copy from sources word-for-word. Never use large language models (LLMs) or generative AI . New here? Creating an article is one of the more difficult tasks on Wikipedia, and you'll have a higher chance of success if you help out with other tasks first to learn more about how Wikipedia works. You can always come back to create an article later; there is no rush ! Article creation Introductory Getting started with Wikipedia Article wizard Your first article Suggested articles Most-wanted articles Requested articles Images needing articles Concepts and guidelines Standard layout Lead section Sections Stub articles Categorization Development processes Article development Moving a page Merging articles Featured article criteria The perfect article Meta tools and groups WikiProject: Articles for creation Special:NewPages Special:NewPagesFeed New pages patrol New articles by topic Recent additions ( DYK ) v t e Welcome to Wikipedia! Creating a new article is one of many ways to contribute to the encyclopedia , but can be difficult for new editors. We recommend looking at our introductory tutorials or contributing to Wikipedia to learn the basics about editing first. Working on existing articles is a great way to learn Wikipedia's protocols and style conventions ; see the Task Center or your homepage for articles that need your assistance and tasks you can help out with. Before creating your first article, it's highly recommended to practice in your sandbox . Choose a topic supported by reliable , independent sources. Write in a neutral tone , avoid promotional language , and make sure all the information in the article is supported by your sources . Don't use large language models to write your articles either. If you're unsure, the Article Wizard can help guide you step-by-step through the process. Don't worry if it's not perfect—every experienced editor started with their first try! Once you are familiar with the basics of Wikipedia editing , this page will guide you through the process of creating your first article ! Specifically, you will learn how to: Determine whether Wikipedia should have a new article on the given subject Identify and use reliable sources to support assertions in the article Create a draft of the article Submit the draft for publication into the encyclopedia itself The basics Further information: Wikipedia:Simplified ruleset , Wikipedia:Reliable sources , Wikipedia:Verifiability , Wikipedia:Citing sources , and Help:Find sources All new articles start by researching a topic using high-quality, published sources . Even if you're an expert on a topic, you can't just write what you know off the top of your head; published sources are needed. High-quality sources include books by reputable publishers, respected newspapers , peer-reviewed scientific and academic journals , and other sources with a reputation for fact-checking and accuracy . This may include some high-quality websites, but excludes personal and company websites, blogs , social media , and any site where the public can contribute , like forums and even Wikipedia itself . We summarize such high-quality, published sources in Wikipedia articles. That is all we do! Please make sure that everything you write on Wikipedia is based on such sources, and be sure to include inline citations along with the content you write. While primary sources can be used, they should be used sparingly and carefully, usually only to support basic facts. Primary sources do not contribute to establishing notability. Before you start writing Are you connected to the article topic? Further information: Wikipedia:Plain and simple conflict of interest guide and Wikipedia:Paid-contribution disclosure If you have a personal or professional relationship with what you want to write about, it is best if you do not create the new article yourself. Editing with a conflict of interest , regardless of whether you feel you can do so neutrally, gives the appearance of bias and undermines public confidence in Wikipedia. If you create an article despite your conflict of interest, you must disclose your relationship and make sure that it is reviewed by another editor by submitting it via Articles for creation . If you have a financial conflict of interest in the topic (for example if you have been paid to edit it) you must make the required paid-contribution disclosure and abide by the community's restrictions on paid editing . Search for an existing article Further information: Help:Searching The English Wikipedia already has 7.3 million articles. Before creating a new one, try to make sure there is not already an article (or a Draft in development) on the same topic, perhaps under a different spelling, or even a different name. Search for articles (or drafts) that already exist: Main Draft Note: Articles are in "Main" space, and drafts are in "Draft" space. If you're sure that there is no article or draft available for your topic, then there is just one big task to do before you start writing your first article: you have to gather sources about the topic to establish its notability . Gather sources Further information: Help:Find sources As described above in § The basics , Wikipedia articles are written based on published sources. If you need some help finding sources, see this helpful guide . For some common sources, you may find these assessments by the Wikipedia community helpful. Please note these assessments certainly do not list all possible sources: if a source is not listed, that only means the community hasn't evaluated it yet. If a source meets the reliable source criteria, you are welcome to use it. If you have questions, please do ask at the Teahouse . Notability – should this topic have an article? Notability General notability guideline Subject-specific guidelines Academics Astronomical objects Books Events Films Geographic features Music Numbers Organizations and companies People Species Sports and athletes Web content See also Notability essays Guide to deletion Common deletion outcomes Why was my article deleted? v t e Main page: Wikipedia:Notability Your topic must meet Wikipedia's criteria for having an article, which we call " notability ". If there are multiple published reliable sources about a topic, then it may be notable. A topic is not notable if there aren't sufficient reliable sources about it. Important: unreliable ones like blogs , social media , and websites anyone can edit don't count! The general notability guideline gives more details on how to tell if a topic is notable or not. If you're not sure if your topic is notable, ask for help at the Teahouse . A notable topic is one that has multiple reliable sources that each meet all three of the following criteria: Secondary . A secondary source provides thought and reflection based on primary sources, generally at least one step removed from a topic. It contains analysis, evaluation, interpretation, or synthesis of the facts, evidence, concepts, and ideas taken from primary sources . Independent of the subject. This means that nobody involved in writing or publishing the source has a financial or other connection to the subject. A source is not independent of the subject if any of the following are true: if the subject paid for it, including all forms of sponsored content , if the content within the source originates from the subject, including most interviews and all press releases , even if published by a third party (sometimes called " churnalism "), or it was published by the subject itself , on behalf of the subject, or by someone related to the subject. Significant coverage . The sources must discuss your subject in depth , in multiple paragraphs. Trivial mentions, such as one or two sentences or the appearance of your subject in a table or list, are not enough to help establish notability. The special notability guideline for businesses has lots of good examples of what is considered significant and trivial . If your topic is not notable, stop here and find a new one. Non-notable topics do not qualify for a separate article. Consider expanding a relevant existing article related to the topic or selecting a new topic. If you are stuck, ask for guidance at the Teahouse . Look at similar articles See also: Help:Introduction to the Manual of Style It's a good idea to look at several existing Wikipedia articles on subjects similar to yours to see how such articles are formatted. The quality of our existing articles varies and lower-quality articles should not be used as a model. The Talk page of the article may have a quality rating in the shaded box at the top. If an article has been assessed as B -class, or as a Good Article or Featured Article , it is safe to use as a template for your article. You can also consult Wikipedia's Manual of Style for guidance on how to structure an article. Writing your draft Further information: Wikipedia:Writing better articles Once you've verified that there § isn't already an article out there about your topic, § gathered your sources , and § established notability , you're ready to start writing! What editing tool to use Edit tab in desktop view Edit pencil in mobile view Further information: Help:Introduction , Help:Wikitext , and Help:VisualEditor Wikipedia provides various editing tools , and you have a choice of what tool best suits your needs: Editing interface selector Source editor – edits the wikitext of the article, which uses some special characters, like adding [ [ square brackets ] ] to create a link to another page, or asterisks to make bullet points. Visual Editor – a tool similar to a word processor, for editing articles without the need to understand any special codes or markup . Visual Editor is the default. To switch your default editing interface, select an option from the "Editing mode" menu in your preferences . Users of mobile devices are automatically redirected to the official mobile version of Wikipedia. If you don't want to use the mobile version, tap the Desktop link at the bottom of any page to switch to the desktop version. Where to start writing Further information: Wikipedia:Drafts and Wikipedia:About the sandbox Where will you develop your draft? You have several options: in " Draftspace " – this is a special area of Wikipedia dedicated to creating new articles, and is a good choice because other editors can find your draft here and help out. in your sandbox – this is a page you can always easily find, by tapping the user icon in the top right corner to show the menu linking your sandbox. Downside: you can only create one article at a time there, and it's not so easy for other editors to find. in other user subpages . The easiest way is with the Article Wizard, which will create your article in Draft space and guide you through the steps of creating a draft. Create your draft with the Article Wizard! How to create content Further information: Help:Editing , WP:Neutral point of view , and WP:Verifiability Writing a Wikipedia article: Summarize the most important things your sources say. Don't copy wording from your sources; instead, summarize the ideas in the source using your own words. Summarization is more than just changing a few words around here and there. Only add information supported by your sources . Don't add from your own knowledge or expertise. Make sure you show all major viewpoints fairly. Do not cover fringe views or those held only by a tiny minority. Don't take sides or use promotional language . Write in a professional tone ; avoid loaded language. Add citations as you go. This is much easier than writing first and trying to remember later where you found each piece of information. You don't have to write the article all at once! Save your progress frequently, with an appropriate edit summary . The Publish changes… button saves your progress. You can add images , templates like an infobox and categories at the bottom of your article. Don't use large language models ("AI") like ChatGPT to generate article content. These often produce inaccurate text and sometimes make up fake sources and references. It is much better to write the article completely yourself, so that you can be confident in what it says. Remember, you are responsible for the content you add. Citing sources Further information: Wikipedia:Citing sources , Help:Find sources , Help:Referencing for beginners , and Help:Introduction to referencing with VisualEditor Sources are the published books, academic articles, reputable magazines and newspapers, and other locations where you find the information you will be writing about. You will need to find sources before you start writing, because all content in articles at Wikipedia must be verifiable —that is, backed up by reliable sources . The best way to demonstrate verifiability is by creating a citation to a reliable source that you found, and embedding it in-line as you write your article. The best sources tend to have some form of editorial oversight and a reputation for fact-checking and accuracy. Some websites are reliable; many are not. If you're not sure about the reliability of a website, you can read what editors think about them . It's okay to use non-English sources , offline sources , and subscription-only or fee-based sources , as long as they are reliable. Dos and don'ts Main pages: Wikipedia:What Wikipedia is not and Wikipedia:Avoiding common mistakes Here are some "Do"s and "Don't"s, to highlight some of the most important points about writing your first article: Dos and don't Great ways to contribute Things to avoid Do make sure that the topic you write about is notable ; articles about non-notable topics get deleted. Do include citations to independent , reliable sources for all assertions of fact. Do add content that has a neutral point of view , and fairly represents the majority of the sources. Do exercise caution when editing articles about living people . Negative or critical content must be impeccably sourced to highly reliable sources . Do ask for help at the Teahouse , the Help desk , or check these help links . Don't engage in original research or personal essays. Don't copy copyrighted material into articles. Don't speculate about events in the future . Don't write an article only to define a word; Wikipedia is not a dictionary . Try Wiktionary instead. Don't write an article if you have a conflict of interest because of a personal or professional connection. Don't use large language models (LLMs) to write original content. Publish your draft When your draft is ready, you have two options for publishing it: you can do so directly yourself, or ask another editor to review it first. If you don't have an account, if your account is not yet confirmed , or if you have a conflict of interest with the article topic, you will have to ask for a review. Otherwise, the choice is up to you. In either case, you should take some time to double-check that the draft is ready first. Pre-publication checks Take another look at your draft to see if it meets the criteria required for a Wikipedia article. Make sure that: The first sentence defines the article topic, and tells the reader who or what the subject is in plain English. There are citations to reliable sources in the article (most reviewers look for at least three sources). Some specific types of information require inline citations , namely: direct quotations , and any contentious material about living persons (negative, positive, or neutral). The article is written from a neutral point of view . Any controversial claims about living people are impeccably sourced. Publish directly Main page: Wikipedia:Drafts § Moving drafts to mainspace If you are sure your draft is ready, and you do not have a § conflict of interest with the topic , you can publish it directly by moving the page from the draft namespace to the main article namespace. To do so, follow the instructions in how to move a page . Ask for a review Further information: Wikipedia:Articles for creation Alternatively, if If you think your article is ready but would like another editor to check it , you can submit it for review by an experienced editor by clicking the Submit the draft for review! button at the top of your draft. If the button isn't there, you can instead add { { subst:submit } } to the top of the draft. A reviewer will then look at your draft and either publish it or give you feedback on how to improve it. You may continue to edit the page, even while waiting for a review. This may take some time (maybe weeks); please have patience, we are all volunteers. Congratulations! Congratulations, you've created your first article! We have some suggested next steps at Help:After your first article , but do pat yourself on the back. Not many people have successfully created an article on Wikipedia! Help is available! One of the best places to ask for assistance is at the Teahouse , which is dedicated to answering newer editors' questions. Contact your Wikipedia mentor – they are there to answer your questions! For an overview of our policies and guidelines, see Everything you need to know . For a list of informative, instructional and supportive pages, see the Help directory . More can be found at the request directory . Click here to ask for help on your talk page . A volunteer will visit you there shortly! Alternatively, you can ask a question via the #help channel at Wikipedia:Discord or IRC chat at the # wikipedia-en-help connect channel. Further information can be found at the DYK guidelines . Nominate an article Frequently asked questions [ edit ] How do I write an interesting hook? Successful hooks tend to have several traits . Most importantly, they share a surprising or intriguing fact. They give readers enough context to understand the hook, but leave enough out to make them want to learn more. They are written for a general audience who has no prior knowledge of or interest in the topic area. Lastly, they are concise, and do not attempt to cover multiple facts or present information about the subject beyond what's needed to understand the hook. When will my nomination be reviewed? This page is often backlogged. As long as your submission is still on the page, it will stay there until an editor reviews it. Since editors are encouraged to review the oldest submissions first, it may take several weeks until your submission is reviewed. In the meantime, please consider reviewing another submission (not your own) to help reduce the backlog (see instructions below ). Because of WP:DYKTIMEOUT , a nomination should be reviewed within two months since the reviewer/promoter may agree to reject and close an unpromoted hook after that time has passed. Where is my hook? Shortcut WP:DYKFIND WP:DYKFIND If you can't find the nomination you submitted to this nominations page, it may have been approved and is on the approved nominations page waiting to be promoted. It could also have been added to one of the prep areas , promoted from prep to a queue , or is on the main page. If the nominated hook is in none of those places, then the nomination has probably been rejected. Such a rejection usually only occurs if it was at least a couple of weeks old and had unresolved issues for which any discussion had gone stale. If you think your nomination was unfairly rejected, you can query this on the DYK discussion page or with the closer, but as a general rule such nominations will only be restored in exceptional circumstances. If your nomination was promoted, but it hasn't reached the main page after two weeks, you can also query this on the DYK discussion page. Instructions for reviewers [ edit ] Main page: Wikipedia:Did you know/Reviewer instructions Any editor who was not involved in writing/expanding or nominating an article may review it by checking to see that the article meets all the DYK criteria ( long enough , new enough , no serious editorial or content issues ) and the hook is cited. Editors may also alter the suggested hook to improve it, suggest new hooks, or even lend a hand and make edits to the article to which the hook applies so that the hook is supported and accurate. For more information on the DYK rules and review processes, see the DYK guidelines and the reviewer instructions . To post a comment or review on a DYK nomination, follow the steps outlined below: Look through this page, Template talk:Did you know , to find a nomination you would like to comment on. Click the "Review or comment" link at the top of the nomination. You will be taken to the nomination subpage. The top of the page includes a list of the DYK criteria. Check the article to ensure it meets all the relevant criteria. To indicate the result of the review (i.e., whether the nomination passes, fails, or needs some minor changes), leave a signed comment on the page. Please begin with one of the 5 review symbols that appear at the top of the edit screen, and then indicate all aspects of the article that you have reviewed; your comment should look something like the following: Article length and age are fine, no copyvio or plagiarism concerns, reliable sources are used. But the hook needs to be shortened. If you are the first person to comment on the nomination, there will be a line :* <!-- REPLACE THIS LINE TO WRITE FIRST COMMENT, KEEPING :* --> showing you where you should put the comment. Save the page. After the nomination is approved, a bot will automatically list the nomination page on Template talk:Did you know/Approved . If there is any problem or concern about a nomination, please consider notifying the nominator by placing {{subst:DYKproblem|Article|header=yes|sig=yes}} on the nominator's talk page. Promoters should not promote their own nomination or their own review. When promoting hooks intended for a particular date, keep in mind that when the number of available approved nominations exceeds 120 we switch to two sets per day , and when that number drops below 60 we return to one set per day . In the window where the DYK nomination subpage is open, replace the line {{DYKsubpage with {{ subst: DYKsubpage , and replace | passed = with | passed = no . Then save the page. This has the effect of wrapping up the discussion on the DYK nomination subpage in a blue archive box and stating that the nomination was unsuccessful, as well as adding the nomination to a category for archival purposes. Alternatively, you can use PSHAW , which automates the process. How to remove a hook from the prep areas or queue [ edit ] Edit the prep area or queue where the hook is and remove the hook and the credits associated with it. Go to the hook's nomination subpage (there should have been a link to it in the credits section). View the edit history for that page Go back to the last version before the edit where the hook was promoted, and revert to that version to make the nomination active again. Add a new icon on the nomination subpage to cancel the previous tick and leave a comment after it explaining that the hook was removed from the prep area or queue, and why, so that later reviewers are aware of this issue. Add a transclusion of the template back to this page so that reviewers can see it. It goes under the date that it was first created/expanded/listed as a GA. You may need to add back the day header for that date if it had been removed from this page. If you removed the hook from a queue, it is best to either replace it with another hook from one of the prep areas, or to leave a message at WT:DYK asking someone else to do so. How to move a nomination subpage to a new name [ edit ] Don't; it should not ever be necessary, and will break some links which will later need to be repaired. Even if you change the title of the article, you don't need to move the nomination page. For the 50 Cent song, see Candy Shop . For The Two Ronnies sketch, see The Two Ronnies § Notable sketches . Admins, do not protect this page Learn why: Only admins can see this message. This article is currently featured on the Main Page as This Week's Article for Improvement . The purpose of TWAFI is to encourage readers of the Main Page to make their first edits and understand how Wikipedia works. Keeping this article completely unprotected is essential to this goal. Obviously, we need a lot of eyes to watch out for vandalism, but an increase in vandalism is not a reason to protect TWAFI. Instead, monitor this article closely and block specific problematic accounts rather than restricting access for unregistered users or applying pending changes protection. Move protection is ok for the entire week to prevent page move vandalism. This is Wikipedia's current article for improvement: please help us edit it ! Here are some suggestions: Work to keep the article focused on the topic . It should not discuss the general history of confectionery itself, only the stores that sell them. The lead section needs cleanup, probably a general rewrite You can read our editing tutorial , or start improving the article right away . You can also suggest changes to this article, or ask for help . An American candy store and an Austrian Konditorei ( top ), a Welsh pick-and-mix sweet shop ( middle ), a Turkish confectionery store and a Moroccan sweets stall ( bottom ). A confectionery store (also known as a sweet shop , candy store , or lolly shop ) is a speciality store that sells confections , usually focusing on sugar confectionery . They sell candy , candied fruits and nuts , chocolates , locally manufactured sweets, international delicacies, and "vintage" and "classic" varieties such as rock candy , chewing gum and liquorice . [ 1 ] [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ] Confectionery stores have traded for over 1,000 years , selling and sometimes making confections on site. [ 6 ] Dedicated confectionery stores are popular small businesses in many countries due to their low start-up costs, high markup potential, and diverse appeal. [ 7 ] [ 8 ] Confectionery stores have existed dating back to the Song dynasty in China and Classical Japan , and later developments occurred in Mamluk Egypt and Safavid Iran . In early modern Europe, sweet dishes developed from being primarily medicinal to luxurious treats in their own right. By the year 1800, the role of the modern confectioner had emerged. The development of mass production in the 19th century enabled the creation of specialist machinery, which lowered the price of confectionery; this made items like candies able to be sold and produced in quantity, and more available and affordable to most economic classes. The modern era has seen the development of bulk confectionery and worldwide specialisations differentiating the confectionery trade across countries. [ 9 ] History [ edit ] "The Great Buddha Sweet Shop" from Ritō Akizato's Miyako meisho zue (1787) Early history [ edit ] Stores and stalls have sold confections for well over a thousand years. Sugar and sweets were readily available in various Chinese cities during the Song dynasty (960–1279). [ 10 ] Shops in Kaifeng sold children's treats like candied fruits , shrimp whiskers (pulled sugar) and thick sweets. [ 11 ] [ 12 ] In Hangzhou , vendors sold sugar and honey cakes, shaped candies, spun sugar , sweet pastes and syrup. [ 10 ] In Kyoto , Japan, the confectionery shop Ichimonjiya Wasuke , also known as Ichiwa, is traditionally dated to around 1000 CE and continues to sell mochi to shrine visitors. [ 13 ] Located near Imamiya Shrine , its speciality is aburi-mochi ( あぶり餅 ), which are grilled rice cakes coated in sweet miso sauce . [ 6 ] In the mid-ninth to early-tenth century in Persia , the almond-sugar confection marzipan began to be recommended by the physician Rhazes as a remedy for illness. [ 14 ] By the 13th century, marzipan was often sold and traded with foreigners. Within a century, it was consumed by nobility as an early form of confectionery; not long after, it began to be fashioned in intricate, fanciful shapes and served at royal courts. [ 14 ] Marzipan is sold in many confectionery stores to this day, especially during the traditional winter holiday seasons. [ 15 ] In Egypt , increasingly large-scale sugar production and trade, which began in the 12th century by the Ayyubid dynasty , was developed through the 13th to 16th centuries during the Mamluk Sultanate . [ 16 ] Confectioners in Cairo sold a variety of sweets, many with nuts or seeds but not usually fruits. Sugar figurines filled the markets during the month of Rajab and were widely purchased as gifts. [ 17 ] Sephardic Jews fleeing the Inquisition in the 1500s brought their chocolate making to France . [ 18 ] [ 19 ] In Isfahan , Iran , confectionery markets sold sweets to accompany coffee during the Safavid era (1501–1736). [ 20 ] 16th–18th centuries [ edit ] The Female Confectioner (1695) by Nicolas II de Larmessin, part of a satirical series about trades in Paris. Starting in the 16th century, wealthy European meals often ended with sweet dishes , giving rise to occupations dedicated to sweets, including gingerbread makers, sugar bakers and pie bakers. Apothecaries also processed herbs and fruits into preserved sweets for medicinal purposes. Modern confectionery stores developed from the convergence of these trades, as taste and attitudes towards sweets shifted through the 17th and 18th centuries. Once seen as primarily medicinal, sweets were increasingly understood and sold as a luxurious treat. [ 21 ] As colonial sugar production increased, sugar prices declined during the 18th century, and confections became cheaper and more accessible to the middle classes of Europe and the Americas. [ 22 ] La Mère de Famille, which opened in Paris in 1761, is among the oldest surviving confectionery shops in the city. [ 23 ] By 1800, the role of the modern confectioner or sweet maker emerged. [ 24 ] 19th century to present [ edit ] In the 19th century, the development of specialised machinery, such as revolving steam pans and lozenge machines, enabled the mass production and accessibility of confections to poorer consumers. [ 25 ] Sugary confections became more associated with commercial shops with their greater variety of flavours and textures, and less associated with the more limited offerings of the home kitchen. By the late 1800s, sugar prices had fallen further, easing production costs. [ 26 ] In the late 19th century, shops began offering bulk confectionery , typically individually-wrapped and sold in large self-serve containers; in the United States, this was often referred to as "penny candy", [ 27 ] [ 28 ] while in the United Kingdom it was known as "pick and mix". [ 29 ] In the 20th century, confectionery stores started to expand worldwide when as development and production improved, with new products. [ 30 ] In the early 21st century, candy shops became integrated in the concession sections of some movie theatres in the United States. [ 31 ] Tourism [ edit ] A selection of Blackpool rock in different flavours While children are the primary consumers of sugar candy, nostalgia may bring adult customers to confectionery shops. [ 32 ] Large confectionery stores opened in the 21st century, including Candylicious in 2009 at the Dubai Mall , which has an area of 10,000 ft 2 (930 m 2 ) . [ 33 ] Opened in 2011, the M&M's World shop in London is the world's largest confectionery shop at around 35,000 ft 2 (3,300 m 2 ) . [ 34 ] Brussels Airport has the highest chocolate sales in the world, with travellers purchasing an average of 500 g (18 oz) of chocolate every 15 seconds, or 650 tonnes a year. [ 35 ] Attractions such as Cadbury World , in Birmingham, UK, and Hershey's Chocolate World in Pennsylvania, United States, offer factory tours and tastings. [ 36 ] Around the world [ edit ] Local specialities [ edit ] See also: List of candies Confectionery stores often stock regional confections such as Mexican cochinito de piloncillo , British Blackpool rock , [ 37 ] or Southeast Asian dodol , [ 38 ] as well as regional variations of confections like fudge , gumdrops or hard candies . [ 39 ] Some stores ( chocolateries ) only sell varieties of chocolate and similar products. [ 40 ] Others focus on novelty candies (such as promotionally-oriented snacks or unusual flavours [ 41 ] ), items such as flavoured popcorn , or toffees . [ 42 ] [ 43 ] Stores may target specific consumer demographics , such as teenagers, wealthy consumers or tourists. [ 44 ] They may have specialities like allergy-free selections, sugarless candies, or vegan products. [ 45 ] Africa [ edit ] Egypt [ edit ] During the Mamluk Sultanate (1250–1517), Cairo had a specialised market for confectionery known as the Sūq al-Ḥalāwīyīn (Sugar Candy Market). The Egyptian historian Al-Maqrizi (1342–1442) described the market as a commercial centre where shops sold a variety of colored sugar candies alongside metalware and other goods. During the Islamic month of Rajab , confectioners produced elaborate sweets shaped like horses, lions, cats, and other animals. These confections, which ranged in weight from approximately 110 grams to 4.5 kilograms, were suspended by threads in shop displays and purchased for children. Al-Maqrizi noted that similar sweets were sold throughout Cairo, Fustat , and the surrounding areas. He also recorded a decline in confectionery production beginning in the late 14th century, attributing it to disruptions in sugar production and refining, rising sugar prices, and the loss of skilled confectioners. [ 16 ] By the first quarter of the 15th century, the Sūq al-Ḥalāwīyīn had disappeared. [ 46 ] By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, packaged confectionery was also sold through department stores in Egypt, many of which had been established by immigrant merchants. Modern department-store retail in Cairo and Alexandria developed through commercial networks maintained by Levantine Syrian, Sephardi Jewish , and Ashkenazi Jewish families. Among these businesses was Orodsi-Back , founded by Leon Orosdi, a Hungarian émigré who fled the unsuccessful Hungarian Revolution of 1848 . After establishing a store in Istanbul in 1855, Orosdi expanded into Cairo in 1856, opening a business in the Muski commercial district. The company subsequently developed into a department-store chain, expanding beyond clothing into household goods and groceries, including biscuits and chocolate. [ 47 ] During the early 20th century, confectionery was also sold by itinerant street vendors in Cairo. In the 1920s and 1930s, street hawkers travelled regular routes through residential neighbourhoods, using distinctive, melodic calls to advertise their goods. Candy vendors sometimes appealed directly to children, crying out, "Cry to your mother, little boy," to encourage them to ask their mothers for money to purchase sweets. Customers could purchase goods from their apartment windows or balconies by lowering baskets attached to ropes, allowing transactions without descending to the street. [ 48 ] Asia [ edit ] China [ edit ] White Rabbit candies for sale at a confectionery store In China, wedding candy ( Chinese : 喜糖 ; pinyin : xǐtáng ; lit. ' happy candy ' ) [ 49 ] stores grew popular in the 1990s. Zigu Road in Jiangxi had over 20 wedding candy shops, including shops like White Rabbit Creamy Candies, a company based in Shanghai. White Rabbit candies gained popularity throughout the country for their soft, chewy texture and sweet taste. As a result, Chinese confectioneries still use the signature name "Shanghai Candies" to this day. Southern provinces such as Jiangsu , Zhejiang , Fujian and Anhui accounted for nearly 80% of the national wedding confectionery store share, according to food critic Zhu Danpeng. [ 50 ] [ 51 ] It was a thriving new market that business owners competed in, to the point that they crammed shops with candy and displayed sweets outside the doors and into the streets for consumers. [ 51 ] Declining sales amid factors such as the COVID-19 pandemic , falling marriage rates, and increased demand for healthier fruit- and nut-based snacks have driven Chinese confectionery stores to target a wealthier consumer base with imported chocolates and biscuits. [ 52 ] [ 53 ] A sugar painter's stall in Hainan Province Sugar painting is an art form practised by street vendors in Sichuan and the surrounding area. The customer, usually a child, will first spin a wheel to see what form the seller will make. The seller will take liquid sugar in a spoon and drizzle it in a single line onto a slab of marble to make shapes such as birds, fish, dogs, dragons, or even solid forms like bicycles or flower baskets. If it is a flat piece, it will be put on a stick, or wrapped in plastic and given to the customer. This has to be done very quickly, or the sugar will become too hard to work. Sugar painting requires a very significant level of expertise. [ 54 ] India [ edit ] Further information: Sweets from the Indian subcontinent A mix of barfi and peda, two types of traditional sweets, in Chennai , India In India, confectioners are known as halwai , and shops selling traditional sweets are commonly known as mithai shops. In Hindi, mithai ki dukan ( मिठाई की दुकान ) means "sweet shop". The majority of Indian sweets are milk-based, such as barfi . Their offerings vary by region; Agra is known for petha , a sweet made from ash gourd, while Mathura is known for peda . Kolkata has a long-established tradition of sweet shops selling Bengali sweets such as sandesh , as well as seasonal preparations such as pithe . [ 55 ] [ 56 ] Japan [ edit ] In the Edo period , confectionery stores bore the symbol of paulownia and swirling patterns, and often had an image of Kawaguchiya, one of the two main candy brands in the An'ei era . Small-scale shops had umbrellas to protect candies from melting or getting wet. To increase sales, some vendors wore women's clothing or displayed karakuri puppets . A vendor sang along with a shamisen and was rewarded with clothing bearing the Onoe Kikugorō V family's crest. [ 57 ] In a 1777 listing, there were 28 confectionery stores in Edo (now Tokyo ). Several of them called themselves " kudarikyogashiya " to benefit from an association with " kudarimono ", prized goods from the region of Kamigata . Kyoto meibutsu mizu no fukiyose had confectionery reviews, judging their specialities, product colour, degree of steaming for steamed confectionery and even the confectionery's container. [ 58 ] Cafés began to appear in the Meiji era , serving Western sweets and coffee; they developed further during the Taishō era . [ 59 ] Recreation of a dagashiya at Ōme Akasuka Fujio Kaikan Museum (Retro Museum of Packaging from the Showa Era, 1926–1989) Prior to the 1980s, the Japanese custom for purchasing candy took place at a dagashiya ( 駄菓子屋 ), also known as a "trivial sweets shop". When konbini stores began to take root in the late 1980s, the smaller, less-stocked dagashiya market began to face steady competition. [ 60 ] Despite this competition, a number of dagashiya chains managed to survive. One notable example is Okashi no Machioka, known for selling both Western items such as potato chips and chocolate bars, alongside traditional snacks such as yōkan ( 羊羹 ) and umaibō ( うまい棒 ). Some dagashiya stores have been in the same location for centuries. One example is Kami-kawaguchiya, which was established in Zōshigaya and, as of 2026, remained open for over 200 years. [ 60 ] Notable candies sold at Japanese confectioneries include plum-flavoured snacks, jellies, jams, mints, nuts and crackers. Senbei ( 煎餅 ), a type of rice cracker , can also be regularly spotted in shops like these. Seafood is also a very common offering in these shops; iwashi (dried sardines) and ika (dried squid) are very popular snacks. [ 60 ] Korea [ edit ] During the Joseon dynasty, honey and yeot were used to sweeten food while sugar imported in small quantities from China was used primarily as a medicinal ingredient for the royal court and upper classes. In the 1890s, stores in Jongno District began selling candies made from imported sugar. [ 61 ] Malaysia [ edit ] During the early 20th century, traditional coffee shops known as kopitiam became established in British Malaya. Many were operated by Hainanese Chinese immigrants and served coffee alongside local foods and baked goods. Dedicated confectionery businesses subsequently developed, including King's Confectionery, which grew from a family bakery established in the 1960s, and Chiap Tong, a biscuit and candy shop founded in Kuala Lumpur in 1942. [ 62 ] Turkey [ edit ] Confectioneries in Konya from the 13th century are mentioned in the writings of Sufi poet Mevlânâ . Sweets were sold in shops and street stands and occasionally advertised and sold on floats in street processions, as depicted in 16th-century Ottoman miniatures . Parrots were sometimes associated with sweets through verses of mystic poetry in which they desired sweets and would become eloquent, or "sweet-tongued", after consuming sugar. [ 63 ] The Hacı Bekir shop in Istanbul Turkey, and especially its Historical Peninsula , is home to several confectioneries. These stores have been operating since the 18th and 19th centuries. These confectioneries catered to the cosmopolitan upper-middle class who then inhabited the area. These shops can be seen as a result of the Islamic hospitality culture present in Anatolia, where feeding guests and such is seen as a command of the Prophet Muhammad . [ 64 ] [ better source needed ] Some of the oldest surviving confectioneries from this era are Şekerci Cafer Erol, Ali Muhittin Hacı Bekir and Hicipoğlu Şekerleme, which reportedly is the oldest confectionery in Istanbul and has been in operation since 1752. [ 65 ] The Hacı Bekir shop in Istanbul, which opened in 1777, claims to have created the modern Turkish delight ( lokum ). The shop is one of the 100 oldest companies in the world. [ 66 ] [ 67 ] Europe [ edit ] France [ edit ] À la Mère de Famille, one of France's oldest confectionery stores One of France's oldest confiseries , À la Mère de Famille, was founded by Pierre-Jean Bernard and opened in 1761. Candy had been consumed in the country since the Middle Ages , when a man named Regnaut-Barbon founded a guild of confectioners, but it was only eaten by the aristocracy and royalty and used in religious ceremonies. [ 23 ] Germany [ edit ] Traditional Konditorei Fester, est. 1926 in Spandau, Berlin, Germany In Germany, the traditional high-end confectionery shop and café is known as a Konditorei . Unlike a standard retail sweet shop or a bread bakery ( Bäckerei ), a Konditorei specialises in fine baked goods, elaborate tortes, pastries and artisanal chocolates, frequently operating alongside an integrated sit-down café. [ 68 ] Master confectioners ( Konditormeister ) undergo rigorous, regulated vocational training, maintaining a distinction between scratch-made artisanal confections and mass-produced commercial snacks. [ 69 ] The trade's roots stretch deep into the mediaeval European guild system . In Nuremberg , a prominent trading nexus, some of Germany's earliest specialised corporate guilds for fine pastry and spice bakers were established. These included historic Lebküchner (gingerbread and confection) guilds documented as early as the 17th century. [ 70 ] [ 71 ] Over subsequent centuries, these traditions expanded through court confectioners ( Hofkonditoren ) and the opening of early German coffee houses. Over time, the Konditorei matured into a widespread public institution closely tied to the German tradition of Kaffee und Kuchen (coffee and cake), and gradually its offerings expanded to include confectionery such as liquorice, candy canes, marzipan, pralines and gummy candies , leading to the alternative designation "sugar bakery" ( Zuckerbäckerei ). [ 72 ] While dedicated standalone candy shops are relatively rare in modern Germany compared to the Anglo-American world, everyday sweet retail historically operated through general-goods corner stores known as Tante-Emma-Laden [ de ] ("Aunt Emma stores"). [ 73 ] These small neighbourhood shops typically featured glass jars of loose sweets sold individually or compiled into a customised pick-and-mix paper bag, traditionally called a bunte Tüte (mixed bag). Following the decline of general store chains in the late 20th century, this informal sweet-shop role was largely absorbed by street-side kiosks ( Kiosk or Büdchen ) and supermarket chains. [ 74 ] Netherlands [ edit ] A modern Jamin store in the Netherlands Dedicated sweet shops in the Netherlands began to emerge in the 19th century alongside the industrialisation of sugar production. [ 75 ] [ 76 ] Prior to this period, confections were predominantly crafted by apothecaries , who prepared sweets as medicinal remedies, or by specialised sugar bakers ( suikerbakkers ) catering exclusively to the wealthy elite. [ 75 ] The mass production of beet sugar dramatically lowered prices, making sweets widely affordable to the general public and leading to the establishment of the first industrial candy factories and dedicated confectionery retailers across the country. In 1842, Willem Hendrik Fortuin founded Fortuin in Dokkum , which began as a local bakery before expanding into a major confectionery manufacturer known nationally for its peppermints and boiled sweets. [ 77 ] Later, in 1867, Winkeltje Kouwenhoven was established in Delft as a general provisions store, quickly gaining renown for specialising in traditional Dutch sweets and dry goods. [ 78 ] Industrial production of liquorice ( drop ) and peppermint took off in 1878 when Gerrit van Voornveld founded Venco [ nl ] in Amsterdam under the name G. van Voornveld & Co., operating one of the country's first steam-powered candy factories. [ 79 ] This manufacturing trend continued into the 20th century with the establishment of Red Band [ nl ] in Roosendaal by T.J. Overwater in 1928, which rapidly grew into one of the region's prominent producers of sugar confectionery and liquorice. [ 80 ] The defining retail model for Dutch confectionery stores was established by Cornelis Jamin [ nl ] . Jamin began trading sweets as a street vendor in Rotterdam in 1870, before establishing two small sugar processing facilities in 1880 and opening his first official retail confectionery shop in 1883. [ 81 ] In 1886, Jamin scaled up production significantly by opening the Zuid-Hollandsche Stoomfabriek van Koek, Banket, Chocolade en Suikerwerken in Rotterdam. [ 82 ] His retail chain experienced rapid expansion, growing from 50 stores in 1907 to around 300 locations by the 1930s, eventually reaching a peak of over 600 stores nationwide operating under a unified retail format during the 1950s and 1960s. [ 83 ] Russia [ edit ] Russian confectionery shops have served as both manufacturing facilities and stores. The growth of such places took place in the 19th century after the establishment of large chocolate manufacturing enterprises by entrepreneurs from Europe and within the country, [ 84 ] such as Einem (then the nationalised Red October sweet factory ), [ 85 ] Abrikosov (then Babaevsky ), [ 86 ] and Lenov (then Rot Front brand ). After their nationalisation during the Soviet period, these retail stores became the main distribution channels of confectionery produced by state enterprises. [ 87 ] Sweden [ edit ] Sweden has a unique culture surrounding the consumption of candy, with the majority of it being purchased on Saturdays due to the tradition of lördagsgodis emerging in the 1950s as a response to dental issues facing the population. Relegating candy consumption to one day a week was a solution to the rise of tooth decay. [ 88 ] Swedish candy is typically pick-and-mix style, sold at dedicated confectionery stores and grocery stores. Candies sold at Swedish stores include many forms of liquorice, gummies, and sour candies. Liquorice specifically is largely associated with Sweden and other Scandinavian countries. Swedish candy stores are beginning to pop up in other parts of the world such as the United States. [ 89 ] Switzerland [ edit ] See also: Swiss chocolate Switzerland is home to many confectionery chains, and luxury chocolate has become associated with the country. [ 90 ] These stores are owned by manufacturers such as Lindt [ 91 ] and Confiserie Sprüngli . [ 92 ] Chocolate was introduced to Europe following Spanish contact with the Americas by the colonisation of South America in the sixteenth century, and Switzerland developed its own chocolate-making industry that expanded during the nineteenth century through innovations in manufacturing and the development of milk chocolate. [ 90 ] [ 93 ] Beginning in the 18th century, cafes became fashionable places to purchase and consume chocolate and confectionery. [ 94 ] Confectionery stores began gaining traction in the 19th century with the invention of milk chocolate and dark chocolate (through the process of conching ) by Daniel Peter in 1875 [ 93 ] and Rodolphe Lindt in 1879, respectively. [ 90 ] [ 95 ] One such Swiss confectionery store is the Confiserie Sprüngli branch in Zurich , notable for its chocolate and other confectionery such as the Luxemburgerli , a type of macaron . [ 96 ] United Kingdom [ edit ] Pic'n'Mix at a Woolworths store in Eastleigh , Hampshire (2008) Sugared sweets became popular in the Tudor period , with comfits made from sugared spices, seeds and nuts. These were connected to apothecaries , who would offer sweets to disguise the taste of medicines. [ 97 ] Dedicated sweet shops originated during the 19th century, which featured lavish architecture and catered to wealthy clientele. [ 98 ] The Oldest Sweet Shop in Pateley Bridge , England opened in 1827 and claims to be the longest continuously open seller of aniseed balls , liquorice and sherbet flying saucers in the world, as well as the oldest sweet shop in England. [ 99 ] The oldest continuously operating sweet shop in Scotland is the Star Rock Shop, which opened in Kirriemuir in 1833. [ 100 ] The gradual reduction and eventual abolition of sugar duties in the UK during the 19th century contributed to an increase in the number of sweet shops in Britain. [ 101 ] [ 102 ] In the early 19th century, sweets were produced locally for individual shops with few quality controls, and were often adulterated using cheap substances in order to bring down the price. [ 103 ] [ 104 ] The 1858 Bradford sweets poisoning , in which 20 people died after a sweetmaker accidentally adulterated sweets with arsenic instead of gypsum , led to the introduction of the Adulteration of Food or Drink Act 1860 . [ 105 ] [ 106 ] Woolworths dominated confectionery retailing in the UK, starting in 1909 by selling loose sweets by weight, which were known as Pic'n'Mix. Sweets were initially sourced from New York, but UK factories such as Barker and Dobson and Cadbury's soon became the main suppliers. [ 29 ] This was part of a trend away from dedicated sweet shops towards confectionery sections in general stores such as Woolworths and later in the aisles of supermarkets, as shopping habits changed throughout the 20th century. Smaller sweet shops began to disappear from high streets and villages; by around 2010, a sweet shop had become a relatively uncommon sight. More recently, due to nostalgia, tourist appeal and the ability to advertise through social media, the dedicated sweet shop has made something of a comeback. [ 107 ] Some newer American-themed confectionery stores in the United Kingdom have been investigated by authorities over suspected tax evasion, money laundering, counterfeit goods, and other regulatory violations. [ 108 ] [ 109 ] North America [ edit ] Canada [ edit ] The historic Rogers Chocolates in Victoria, BC In 1885, Charles W. Rogers founded a shop in Victoria, British Columbia , initially selling staples along with confections. The shop quickly became so popular that it had to ration its boxes of chocolates to one per customer. By 1917, it had moved to a larger brick building (the Rogers Building ), where it operates to this day. Frank O'Connor founded the first Laura Secord Candy Store in 1913. By 1924, his business was described by The Financial Post as the world's largest chain of candy shops, with 46 Laura Secord stores. [ 110 ] United States [ edit ] Prior to the mid-19th century, sweets consisted of fruits or nuts flavoured with spices or sweeteners, typically sold by grocers or specialised confectioners. The Shane Confectionery in Philadelphia Philadelphia , Pennsylvania, was home to the Caribbean sugar trade in the late 18th century. Thousands of French-speaking refugees moved there beginning in 1790, fleeing revolutions in France and Haiti, some establishing confectioneries. In 1816, there were over 20 confectioners in Philadelphia, which rose to about 200 in 1857. About half specialised in what is now called candy and the other half in different treats, including pastries, ice cream and jellies. [ 111 ] The Industrial Revolution in the mid-19th century allowed for sugar-based candies to be mass-produced. This made sweet treats affordable to more people. Also around this time, chocolate, which had previously generally been consumed unsweetened in the United States, became popular as a candy. [ 111 ] "Ye Olde Pepper Candy Companie" in Salem, Massachusetts , the oldest candy shop in the United States, [ 112 ] was founded in 1806 by Mary Spencer. [ 113 ] [ 114 ] In the late 19th century, confectionery stores specialising exclusively in saltwater taffy [ 115 ] started to become popular, primarily in New Jersey and north eastern coastal areas. At the same time, fudge , created in northeast America in the last quarter of the 1800s, also began to be sold in speciality confectionery stores in the same area. Saltwater taffy and fudge shops retain their identities as specialised shops and remain popular to this day, where goods made on-site (often where customers can view products being made) may be purchased as souvenirs or gifts. Steel's Fudge, established in New Jersey in 1919, is considered the oldest existing family-owned business specialising in fudge in the United States. [ 116 ] In the southwestern United States , stores selling cactus candy were founded in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. [ 117 ] In the southern United States, in the early 19th century, the American version of pralines was being perfected (modified from recipes originating in France, starting in places such as New Orleans then spreading through the rest of the Southeast). These were sold in southern confectionery shops. In addition, roaming confectioners called "Pralinières", women of lower classes who would make their own confections at home, would walk New Orleans neighbourhood streets selling sweets such as pralines to passers-by. [ 118 ] Pralines are especially prominent in Louisiana , where unique delicacies like praline-flavoured ice cream and bacon are found across the state. A distinctive praline made occasionally without milk or cream was also made in the state. [ 119 ] In the early 20th century, confectioners in the midwestern United States carried penny candy as well as regional specialities such as sauerkraut candy and other varieties of penuche fudges. [ 120 ] These became prevalent starting around 1907 and derived from immigrant confectioners adapting their recipes to Midwestern tastes. [ 120 ] Sauerkraut candy popularity varied, and its manufacture was also limited by wartime shortages and changing preferences; their presence at confectioners peaked through the 1930s. The United States Food and Drug Act of 1906 imposed stricter regulation on the manufacture and sale of food, helping confectionery stores build consumer trust and brand recognition. [ 25 ] [ 121 ] In 1917, Harrisburg, Pennsylvania had 55 confectionery shops for a population of 70,000. [ 122 ] Starting in the 1950s, American confectionery stores adopted highly colourful interiors in the " Googie " style, featuring geometric shapes, bright neon colours and high-contrast palettes to attract customers. [ 27 ] [ 123 ] The popularisation of the soda fountain in drug stores in the early twentieth century paved the way for factory-produced candy to be sold in drug store chains as well, often out-competing independent candy stores. [ 124 ] Philadelphia's candy industry faced a series of acquisitions and closures in the late 20th and early 21st centuries. Some small-scale family shops managed to survive, however, including the oldest continuously operating confectionery shop in the United States, Shane Confectionery. [ 111 ] [ 125 ] In 2024, there were over 23,000 candy stores across the United States, with Vermont being called "The Candy Capital", with 12.2 confectionery stores per 100,000 residents. [ 126 ] In New York City , despite economic difficulties, candy shops were expanding in June 2026, possibly due to the lipstick effect . [ 127 ] Some candy shops in the United States focus on importing European candies, especially from Sweden; these newer companies include Bonbon, Lil Sweet Treat and Sockerbit. [ 128 ] Oceania [ edit ] Australia [ edit ] Sweet marketing and retailing in Australia developed in the 19th century. In Melbourne , a confectioner's shop operated by William Overton was recorded in 1838. During the second half of the 19th century, confectionery manufacturing expanded, with larger producers emerging: James & Robert Black, Dillon & Barfoot, and T. H. Nott. [ 129 ] In the 20th century, manufacturers including MacRobertson's , Hoadley's Chocolates , and A. W. Allen became prominent in the industry. During World War 1, restrictions on British sweet exports and import duties expanded the market for Australian brands. [ 129 ] Confectionery was traditionally sold in shops known as milk bars . These establishments were popular meeting places, which sold loose sweets, including boiled sweets, liquorice, toffees, sherbets, and jelly sweets, as well as other food. Their prominence declined as supermarkets were introduced and schools operated their own food booths . [ 129 ] [ 130 ] Local speciality products include Violet Crumble , Cherry Ripe , and Allen's Freckles, alongside internationally marketed brands. Confectionery is now distributed predominantly through supermarkets and other general retailers, although specialist and traditional chocolate shops still operate. [ 129 ] [ 131 ] In Brisbane , Tom's Confectionery Warehouse operates as the country's largest sweet shop. In 2023, Tom's Confectionery opened a store in Melbourne's Highpoint Shopping Centre and won the Guinness World Record for largest bulk confectionery (or pick and mix) selection, with 947 varieties of sweets. [ 132 ] Chocolate accounts for approximately 67.3% of Australia's confectionery market value, marketed at US$3.46 billion in 2024.
