The conflict ended temporarily following a ceasefire between the Twic Dinka and Ngok Dinka in May 2023. In September 2023, attacks flared up in the border area between Abyei and Twic County between Twic Dinka and Ngok Dinka youth, with several massacres against Ngok Dinka. Prelude [ edit ] Further information: Ethnic violence in South Sudan , Abyei status referendum , and Sudanese conflict in South Kordofan and Blue Nile The Abyei area is inhabited by the Ngok Dinka , a sub-group of the Dinka people who live in South Sudan. [ 2 ] In the early 1900s, Misseriya Arabs moved to the area following the British conquest. [ 3 ] Following the independence of South Sudan from Sudan in 2011, Abyei was left as a disputed area as no side wanted to give up the rich oilfields in the region. [ 4 ] A short war broke out in 2012 over the area, but was resolved by the creation of the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA). As of 2024, South Sudan holds de facto control over the area. [ 4 ] Most inter-communal violence is driven by Misseriya Arabs against the Ngok Dinka. Due to land disputes between the nomadic Misseriya and farming Ngok combined with climate change exacerbating dry seasons, Misseriya Arabs have encroached on Ngok Dinka land for many years. [ 5 ] The Misseriya are also the only group that boycotted the 2013 referendum proposing Abyei fall under South Sudanese control, instead favoring Sudanese rule. [ 6 ] Conflict [ edit ] Initial attacks [ edit ] The first attack happened on February 10, 2022, after Twic Dinka youths were beaten by Ngok Dinka Police who were with Abyei administrators surveying land on the Twic- Twic State . [ 7 ] The surveyors were at the Aneet market whenever the Twic youth sent by Twic tax collectors attacked the surveyors. Four people had been killed by the time UNISFA was sent to relieve tensions. [ 7 ] Twelve others were wounded in the attack. [ 7 ] The death toll later increased to 27 dead and 26 injured, according to Abyei Security Advisor Kiluk Kon. [ 8 ] By March 6, over 50,000 refugees had fled to Abyei town due to the Twic attacks and by an attack in Mading-thon and Kuol Bol by Misseriya Arabs. [ 9 ] Between March and April, attacks occurred in Nong, Lu, and Kolom. The Nong attack killed seven people, the Lu attack killed five and one was injured, and in Kon, four people were killed. Around 2,000 heads of cattle were stolen in Lu as well. [ 8 ] Kon also stated that in the attacks, the perpetrators wore the uniform of the Sudanese Armed Forces. [ 8 ] In May 2022, the SSPDF intervened in the area. South Sudanese President Salva Kiir also announced the creation of a panel to assess and relieve the violence. [ 10 ] Peace talks also began in Entebbe , Uganda in May between Ngok Dinka and Misseriya tribal leaders, sponsored by the Community Empowerment for Progress Organization , a South Sudanese aid organization. [ 11 ] Intensification of the Twic Dinka-Ngok Dinka border conflict [ edit ] Starting in June 2022, and intensifying in September and October 2022, Ngok Dinka and Twic Dinka clashed at the borders of Abyei and Twic states. [ 10 ] The SSPDF intervened a second time, and a CEPO-mediated peace negotiation saw a peace treaty between Twic and Ngok Dinka. [ 12 ] However, fighting re-erupted in December 2022 at the village of Wou Chien on the Abyei-Twic border. [ 12 ] [ 13 ] In January 2023, an attack by around 200 Twic Dinka and Bul Nuer led by former SPLM commander Stephen Buay Rolnyang attacked the Abyei village of Rumamier, killing thirteen civilians and aid workers, and injuring four others. [ 14 ] UNISFA troops intervened, but the village was burnt down. [ 14 ] A week later, three people were killed and two injured by Ngok Dinka militants in Twic State. [ 4 ] On January 27, battles between the Bul Nuer and Ngok Dinka saw several dozen civilians killed and hundreds of cattle stolen in the Abyei villages of Tong Liet, Makoac-Madou, and Makeibum. [ 4 ] Due to the violence, Abyei chief administrator Kuol Deim Kuol resigned after protests. Kuol, however, alleged that officials from Warrap and Abyei were behind the violence. [ 15 ] The new administrator, Chol Deng Alaak , vowed to establish peace. [ 16 ] On February 28, UNISFA denounced the movement of South Sudanese armed forces to Abyei. [ 17 ] A second peace treaty between the Twic Dinka and Ngok Dinka was signed in Wau on April 6. [ 18 ] However, the Ngok Dinka sultan, Belbek Kuol Deng , stated that attacks by Misseriya Arabs still continued against Ngok Dinka communities. [ 19 ] At the outbreak of the War in Sudan on April 15, tensions rose between the Twic, Misseriya, and Ngok Dinka, but no attacks were reported. [ 20 ] On April 9, eleven people were killed in an ambush in Akol Matnyang, Rumamer county, by Rolnyang's South Sudan People's Movement/Army . [ 21 ] War in Sudan and ceasefire [ edit ] The United Nations postponed the deployment of additional peacekeepers in UNISFA to Abyei in May 2023, following the breakout of the war in Sudan. [ 22 ] The UN also expressed concern that the war would collapse the ceasefire that was agreed upon in Abyei, and restart attacks. [ 23 ] Both Sudanese and South Sudanese forces deployed to the area following the war, in violation of the demilitarization delineated in the ceasefire. [ 24 ] A South Sudanese internal report stated that neutral mediators of the 2022–2023 clashes picked sides, and that a neutral mediator of the conflict shouldn't be from Bahr el Ghazal . [ 25 ] Five people were killed and six were injured in the Hafir El Sillik area of Abyei on May 22. Ngok Dinka sultan Deng stated that the Misseriya were not involved in the attack, and other sources stated that an SSPDF-affiliated militia called Titabai was the perpetrator. [ 26 ] That same day, the Ghanaian Battalion of UNISFA had luggage looted en route to Abyei. [ 27 ] Four Twic Dinka were killed and one Abyei civilian was killed in a botched cattle raid attempt by the Twic Dinka on June 21. [ 28 ] Second spate of fighting [ edit ] On September 23, 2023, Twic Dinka attacked a market in Athony, but nobody was killed or injured. A second raid occurred on September 27 in Manyiel Rou, and six cows were stolen and the owner was killed. [ 29 ] That same day, a driver in Buol Kech was killed. [ 30 ] More bandits attacked Nyinkuec on September 30, killing fourteen people and injuring fourteen others. [ 29 ] [ 31 ] Twic County officials claimed that no such attack happened. [ 29 ] Abyei officials imposed a curfew in response to the Nyinkuec attack. [ 32 ] Twic youth attacked Athony again on October 4, killing four Abyei youth and one Twic fighter. Three Abyei civilians were injured. [ 33 ] According to officials in Abyei, instead of a cattle raid, this attack was intended by the Twic to occupy the village. [ 33 ] While SSPDF exercised control of the area after the attack, fears of reprisal attacks were imminent. [ 33 ] Ngok Dinka youth and fighters from Unity State launched a reprisal attack on October 25 in Buombil, Twic County, killing two SSPDF soldiers and three children. Five others were injured as well. [ 33 ] The situation calmed down following the Buombil attack, and no attacks were reported for almost a month. On November 19, 2023, Ngok Dinka fighters attacked an SSPDF base in Ayouk, killing eight soldiers and eleven of their family members, with four Ngok Dinka and Nuer youth killed. [ 34 ] Twic County officials claimed the attack took place in Twic territory, and that thirty-five soldiers and civilians were killed in the attack. Sultan Kuol Deng claimed that the Ayouk raid was instigated by Twic youth and SSPDF fighters, who initially attacked Ngok Dinka in preparation for an attack in Abyei. [ 34 ] SSPDF forces under General Akuei Ajou, who survived the Ayouk raid, attacked civilians in Rumamer and Alal counties on November 19 following the raid. [ 34 ] Twic and SSPDF forces attacked the villages of Angot, Wincuei and Nyiel, killing a Ghanaian peacekeeper, and six fighters. [ 35 ] Abyei officials also accused Gai Machiek's militia called Titweng of aiding the SSPDF and Twic youth. Twenty-seven people were killed in the first attack in Mayot, and the second attack in Maluel Aleu was repulsed by UNISFA intervening against the SSPDF and Titweng. [ 35 ] Twenty people were injured in the attacks, and five were killed in Maluel Aleu as well. [ 35 ] Ajou denied the involvement of the SSPDF during the raids, and called for peace between Twic and Ngok Dinka. [ 36 ] [ 35 ] UNISFA also reported no peacekeepers were killed. [ 35 ] The toll of the attacks grew to forty-seven civilians killed and thirty-four injured, with the affected villages being Ayuok, Athony, Malual Aleu, Ka-dhian, Nyiel, Angot Wuncuei, and Wunpeeth, according to the Abyei Civil Society Organization. [ 37 ] UNISFA urged officials on November 23 to investigate the killings at the Ayouk raid and in the November 19 attacks, and asserted that seventy-five people were killed during the latter. [ 38 ] Protests then broke out on November 27 in towns across Abyei decrying UNISFA's lack of protection of Abyei communities, and for the withdrawal of SSPDF and the Sudanese Armed Forces. [ 37 ] Clashes broke out again between Twic Dinka and Ngok Dinka in Athony and other border villages on December 3, killing six people and injuring thirty-five others. The attacks were reportedly started by Twic raids. [ 39 ] [ 40 ] On December 14, one person was killed and four others injured in border attacks, with both Abyei and Twic officials trading blame. [ 41 ] A similar attack occurred on December 20 on the border, with Abyei officials claiming the deaths of six Twic youth. [ 42 ] On December 31, the deputy administrator of Abyei, Noon Deng, was killed with five others in Rummamer county by unknown gunmen. [ 43 ] Noon Deng's killing was deplored by UNISFA. [ 44 ] On January 2, 2024, fighting broke out between SSPDF's 3rd Division led by Ajou along with Gal Machiek's militia against SSPDF forces led by General Kuel Garang, killing five people and injuring an unknown number more. [ 45 ] Border attacks continued throughout January 2024, mostly with kidnappings and cattle and sheep raids. Attacks were uncommon. [ 46 ] [ 47 ] Gai Machiek's campaign [ edit ] On January 27, 2024, Twic Dinka attacked the border villages of Nyinhuac, Majbong, and Ka-dhian and killed over fifty-three people and injured over sixty-four others. The attack was repelled by UNISFA, who lost two peacekeepers. [ 48 ] [ 49 ] [ 50 ] The perpetrators of the attack were also associated with Gai Machiek. [ 51 ] Between February 3 and 4, Machiek's militia launched attacks on Mijak, Aleel, and Rummamer counties. The first attack occurred at 10:30am in Rummamer county, where one person was killed and one was injured. Further attacks occurred in Mijak county around 3pm, where fourteen people were killed when their houses were burned. [ 52 ] Another attack occurred in Aleel county, leading to the deaths of four civilians, and one in Machbong, where a market was torched. [ 52 ] Nineteen people were killed and eighteen were injured in the February 3 attacks. [ 53 ] Further attacks the next day killed eighteen people and saw Twic Dinka and Gai Machiek's militants steal 1,000 heads of cattle. [ 53 ] Reactions [ edit ] The United Nations called for peace in the region in May 2023. [ 54 ] UNISFA also congratulated the initial ceasefire in April 2023. [ 55 ] Countries China expressed concern that the war in Sudan would restart conflict in Abyei in May 2023. [ 56 ] France called for peace in the region in May 2023. [ 54 ] Supranational organizations The United Nations also expressed concern that the war in Sudan would restart conflict in Abyei in May 2023. text: South Sudan–Sudan relations - Wikipedia Jump to content Search Search South Sudan–Sudan relations 11 languages العربية Thuɔŋjäŋ فارسی עברית Bahasa Indonesia 한국어 Português Русский Српски / srpski ไทย 中文 Edit links From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Bilateral relations Sudan-South Sudan relations Sudan South Sudan Diplomatic mission South Sudan Embassy, Khartoum Sudan Embassy, Juba South Sudan–Sudan relations are the bilateral diplomatic relations between South Sudan and Sudan . The two countries officially established relations on 9 July 2011, following South Sudan's independence. Sudan became the first country in the world to recognize the independence of South Sudan. However, relations between South Sudan and Sudan have remained poor, with both sides supporting rebel groups in each other's territories. The length of the international border between the two countries is 2,158 km. [ 1 ] History [ edit ] Main articles: First Sudanese Civil War and Second Sudanese Civil War This section needs expansion . You can help by adding missing information . ( March 2026 ) Independence of South Sudan [ edit ] Main article: 2011 South Sudanese independence referendum Sudan became the first state in the world to recognise South Sudan as a sovereign state and said it intended to open an embassy in the South Sudanese capital of Juba . On the occasion of South Sudan's independence, Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir spoke to the delegation present for independence celebrations, saying that he "congratulate[s] our brothers and sisters in South Sudan on the occasion of the declaration of their new state and the creation of the State of South Sudan in this dear part of our homeland." [ 2 ] Bilateral relations [ edit ] A brief war erupted in 2012 over the border town of Heglig , home to the Heglig oilfields. Following a six-month conflict, which saw South Sudan briefly enter the area before being pushed back by Sudan, an agreement over the border and mineral sharing was signed. During the Sudanese civil war (2023–present) , South Sudan adopted a mediatory role between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF). [ 3 ] [ 4 ] In February 2025, tensions escalated when the RSF allied with the SPLM–N , a rebel group near the South Sudanese border. [ 5 ] In December 2025, the RSF, SAF, and South Sudan People's Defence Forces signed a tripartite agreement to prevent the conflict from damaging the Heglig oil fields due to the strategic role it plays in Sudan and South Sudan. The South Sudan People's Defence Forces entered the area to maintain security as a neutral party. [ 6 ] [ 7 ] Ongoing disputes [ edit ] See also: Sudanese conflict in South Kordofan and Blue Nile and Ethnic violence in South Sudan Abyei [ edit ] Abyei is administered by Sudan, but also claimed by South Sudan. [ 8 ] Abyei was supposed to have a referendum to determine which country it would be part of, but has been delayed pending discussion of disputes. Kafia Kingi [ edit ] Kafia Kingi is a South Sudan sovereign territory according to the authoritative 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement signed by both states, the UN, and Colin Powell representing the US, but has largely been controlled ever since then by Sudanese forces. The binding 2005 agreement specifies use of the 1 January 1956 boundary. Kafia Kingi was not transferred to Darfur in the north until 1960. Heglig Oilfield [ edit ] Main article: Heglig Crisis The town of Heglig , which is internationally recognised as Sudanese territory but which is also claimed by South Sudan. [ 9 ] Oil transit [ edit ] South Sudan ceased producing oil on a complaint that Sudan was "stealing" its oil en route via pipeline to Port Sudan , the only accessible venue to sell South Sudanese oil beyond Sudan. Sudan responded, saying that it was a "fee" for using the pipeline that was owned by Sudan. Several oil trucks were also briefly held by Sudan but later released saying it was a good faith initiative to lessen tensions. [ 10 ] In September 2012, Sudan and South Sudan agreed a deal on border security and oil production to permit oil exports from South Sudan through Sudan to continue. [ 11 ] In May 2013, Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir threatened again to block oil transits via Sudan if South Sudan continued to support insurgents in South Kordofan and Darfur. [ 12 ] Cultural relations [ edit ] This section needs expansion . You can help by adding missing information . ( March 2025 ) Prior to independence there were also numerous Southern Sudanese, mostly blue collar , workers in the north. At the time of the referendum there was a split on the issue of partitioning the country amid Sudan's claim that they would have to return or apply for work permits. [ 13 ] Economic relations include the transfer of South Sudanese oil via Sudanese pipelines to the Red Sea for export. Bilateral visits [ edit ] The Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir made his first visit to the south on 12 April 2013 since independence. PA00100361 The Hôtel de Ville ( French pronunciation: [ otɛl də vil ] , " City Hall ") is a municipal building in Limoges , Haute-Vienne , France, standing on the Place Jacques Chirac. Completed in 1883 by architect Alfred Leclerc , it was designated a monument historique by the French government in 1975. [ 1 ] It was badly damaged by arson during the 17 October riots . [ 2 ] [ 3 ] History [ edit ] Background [ edit ] By the Middle Ages , the city was managed by consuls based in an ancient town hall in the Rue Fontgrouleu (now the Rue du Consulat), which dated as early as 1487. [ 4 ] [ 5 ] Following the outbreak of the French Revolution , the old building was permanently abandoned and a new town hall was established: the site the council selected was a former convent in the Place Saint-Gérald and earlier an ancient Roman forum . This was a simple two-storey building with a central bell tower, which was completed in 1811. [ 6 ] On 4 April 1871, inspired by the establishment of the Paris Commune , a crowd of revolutionary guardsmen stormed both the town hall and the prefecture, and demanded the establishment of a similar commune in Limoges. In the ensuing melee, shots were fired and Colonel Auguste Billett of the French Army was mortally wounded, although the French Army eventually regained control. [ 7 ] [ 8 ] [ 9 ] Current building [ edit ] After a local resident, Alfred Fournier, died and left his entire estate to the city in July 1875, the council decided to demolish the old town hall and erect a new building on the same site. Winner of the Grand Prix de Rome and former chief architect of the Château de Versailles , Charles-Alfred Leclerc, was commissioned for the project. Construction commenced in 1879 and the building officially opened on 14 July 1883. [ 10 ] In May 1940, during the Second World War , Mayor of Limoges Léon Betoulle , welcomed the prime minister of Belgium , Hubert Pierlot , and other members of the Belgian government in exile to the town hall. [ 11 ] Following the death of the former president of France, Jacques Chirac , in September 2019, the address of the town hall was changed to the Place Jacques Chirac in 2022. [ 12 ] 2026 arson attack [ edit ] The Hôtel de Ville in Limoges collapsing in flames During the 17 October riots , the town hall was attacked by rioters, who stormed the building and threw firebombs inside. [ 13 ] [ 14 ] According to Mayor Guillaume Guérin , after entering the building perpetrators threatened to kill officials and security guards. [ 15 ] The bell tower and roof were consumed by flames and collapsed into the building. [ 2 ] [ 16 ] Firefighters reported that they were able to save four-fifths of the building, but partial collapse of the structure remained possible. [ 17 ] Guérin said he would resign unless the French government paid for the reconstruction. Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu responded that the state would pay for the reconstruction and the continuation of local services in Limoges. [ 18 ] [ 15 ] On 20 October, a 34-year-old activist with a prior history of violence was arrested by French police for the arson attack. [ 19 ] Fire at the Hôtel de Ville (17 October 2026) The day after the fire (18 October 2026) Architecture [ edit ] Inspired by the Hôtel de Ville, Paris , Leclerc designed the building in the Neo-Renaissance and Louis XIII styles , with a symmetrical château -style main frontage of 11 bays facing onto the Place Jacques Chirac. The central section featured a series of tall carriage arches on the ground floor, fenestrated by tall casement windows with balustrades on the first floor. At roof level, there was a parapet , which was decorated with four medallions, and a central clock tower with an ornate belfry , which stood at 43 metres (141 ft) high before the 2026 fire. The end sections of three bays each were fenestrated in a similar style and surmounted by separate mansard roofs . The medallions on the parapet were created by Giandomenico Facchina and depicted the painter Léonard Limosin , the former chancellor Henri François d'Aguesseau , the statesman Pierre Victurnien Vergniaud , and the military leader Jean-Baptiste Jourdan . [ 20 ] The two pediments on either side of the clock were surmounted by statues, sculpted by Tony Noël, representing the industries of goldsmithing and enamelling. [ 21 ] A stone fountain, designed and sculpted by Charles Genuys, was installed in front of the town hall in 1893. [ 22 ] Leclerc incorporated the Neo-Renaissance influence into the interior of the building, with a pink-marble floored reception hall anchored by a sweeping double-flight grand staircase. Murals by Henri-Paul Motte , including Passé et Présent: union du Limousin à la France par Henri IV (exhibited at the 1884 Paris Salon ) and L'Atelier de Léonard Limosin (1885), as well as paintings by Abel Trinocq, Jean-Joseph Weerts , and Urbain Bourgeois were hung throughout the building. Limoges ( / l ɪ ˈ m oʊ ʒ / lih- MOHZH , [ 4 ] [ 5 ] US also / l iː ˈ -/ lee- ; [ 4 ] [ 6 ] French: [ limɔʒ ] ⓘ ; [ 4 ] Occitan : Lemòtges , locally Limòtges [ liˈmɔdzei̯ ] ) is a city and commune , and the prefecture of the Haute-Vienne department in west-central France . [ 7 ] It was the administrative capital of the former Limousin region. Situated on the first western foothills of the Massif Central , Limoges is crossed by the river Vienne , of which it was originally the first ford crossing point. The second most populated town in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region after Bordeaux , a university town , an administrative centre and intermediate services with all the facilities of a regional metropolis, it has an urban area of 323,494 inhabitants in 2022. [ 3 ] The inhabitants of the city are called the Limougeauds. Founded around 10 BC under the name of Augustoritum, it became an important Gallo-Roman city. During the Middle Ages Limoges became a large city, strongly marked by the cultural influence of the Abbey of Saint-Martial , where the Dukes of Aquitaine were invested and crowned. From the 12th century onwards, its enamels were exported throughout the Christian world. In 1765, during the industrial revolution, the discovery of a deposit of kaolin in the Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche region enabled the development of the Limoges porcelain industry. It is sometimes nicknamed "the red city" or "the Rome of socialism" because of its tradition of voting on the left and the workers' events it experienced from the 19th to the beginning of the 20th century. Since the 1990s, the city has had a basketball club, Limoges CSP , which has won several French championships and the European championship in 1993. Because of its heritage policy, it has held the label "City of Art and History" since 2008. Economic activities include butchering , electrical equipment for the building industry , and luxury goods. It is home to porcelain houses and art workshops working with enamel or stained glass . This craft expertise led it to join the UNESCO Creative Cities Network in 2017 in the thematic category "Crafts and Popular Arts". History [ edit ] See also: Timeline of Limoges Ancient and medieval history [ edit ] Scarce remains of pre-urban settlements have been found in the area of Limoges. The capital of the Gaulish people of the Lemovices , who lived in the area, was probably either near Villejoubert , some kilometres southeast of Saint-Léonard-de-Noblat , or Saint-Gence , northwest of Limoges. The city proper was founded as Augustoritum by the Romans , around 10 BC: "rito-" is Gaulish for " ford ". The foundation was part of the reorganization of the province by the emperor Augustus , hence the new name. The Roman city included an amphitheatre measuring 136 x 115 metres, a theatre, a forum , baths and several sanctuaries. According to tradition, a temple consecrated to Venus , Diana , Minerva and Jupiter was located near the modern cathedral. The city was on the typical Roman square plan, with two main streets crossing in the centre. It had a Senate and a currency of its own, a sign of its importance in the imperial age. Later, like many towns and cities in Gaul, it was renamed after the tribe (here the Lemovices ) whose chief town it was; "Lemovices" subsequently evolved into "Limoges", and "Lemovicinus" for the area around changed into " Limousin ". [ citation needed ] Limoges enamel ciborium with champlevé enamel, and center rim in pseudo-Kufic script, c. 1200 [ 8 ] Limoges was evangelized by Saint Martial , who came to the city around 250 with two companions, Alpinianus and Austriclinienus. However, in the late 3rd century it was increasingly abandoned, due to unsafe conditions created by the invasions of various Germanic tribes. The population was concentrated instead in a more easily fortifiable site, the modern Puy Saint-Étienne, which is the centre of the modern Limoges. Starting with the construction of the Abbey of St. Martial (9th century), another settlement grew around the tomb of the saint, while a third area, next to the residence of the viscount (the future Castle of Saint Martial), seems to have been populated from the 10th century. [ citation needed ] Starting from the 11th century, thanks to the presence of the Abbey of St. Martial and its large library, Limoges became a flourishing artistic centre. It was home to an important school of medieval music composition, which is usually called the St. Martial School ; its most famous member was the 13th-century troubadour Bertran de Born . [ citation needed ] In the 13th century, at the peak of its splendour, central Limoges consisted of two fortified settlements. The town proper, with a new line of walls encompassing the Vienne River , inhabited mainly by clerks and workers. It has a bridge on the Vienne river named after Saint-Étienne, built by the bishops, and a developed port. Sacked in 1370, it never recovered entirely. The castle, with 12-metre-high (39 ft) walls, including the abbey controlled by the abbot, sometimes in contrast with the bishop-ruled town ("la Cité"). Traces of the walls can still be seen in the city centre. Outside the lines of walls were the popular quarters. In 1370, Limoges was occupied by Edward of Woodstock, the Black Prince , who massacred some 300 residents, "perhaps a sixth of the normal population", with another 60 members of the garrison of 140 dead as well. [ 9 ] Modern history [ edit ] Yale Mobile Hospital Unit No. 39 stationed at the Limoges factory, Christmas, 1917 Occitan and French name of the city The porcelain industry started to develop, favoured by the presence of kaolinite which was discovered near Limoges in 1768 [ 10 ] (near Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche , southwest of Limoges). Many of the inhabitants became employed in the new sector or in connected activities (including the lumbering of wood needed for firing the porcelain) in manufacture and exporting needed for European distribution of Limoges Boxes , dinnerware, and other porcelain wares. Because the Limousin region has had a long history of breeding (Baronet sheep and Limousine cows ), the leather industry also settled in and around Limoges along the banks of the Vienne–the river providing the necessary water and power. Factories in Limoges and Saint-Junien still produce luxury leather shoes, gloves, and bags. The city and castle were united in 1792 to form the single city of Limoges. During the French Revolution several religious edifices, considered symbols of the Ancien Régime , were destroyed by the population: these included the Abbey of St. Martial itself. [ 11 ] In the 19th century Limoges saw strong construction activity, which included the destruction and rebuilding of much of the city centre. The unsafe conditions of the poorer population is highlighted by the outbreak of several riots, including that of July–November 1830 and April 1848. The first French confederation of workers, the Confédération Générale du Travail (CGT; General Confederation of Labour ), was created in Limoges in 1895. [ citation needed ] In early 1905, strikes began in another local industry, shoe factories soon followed in the porcelain factories. Barricades were built, the army intervened. There would be two casualties: a horse and a young porcelain worker, Camille Vardelle. [ citation needed ] Limoges' historic city hall collapsing in flames, October 2026 During World War II , many Jews from Alsace were evacuated to Limoges and the surrounding area. The 2nd SS Panzer Division Das Reich was stationed near Saint-Junien. After meetings in Limoges and Saint-Junien, the decision was made to carry out the Oradour-sur-Glane massacre on 10 June 1944. This division's mission was to free another battalion commander, Major Helmut Kämpfe , who was later executed on the orders of Georges Guingouin . A monument designed by the artist Sanfourche commemorates these events in Moissannes . Limoges was liberated on 21 August 1944 by the French Resistance led by Colonel Guingouin, without any fighting, after negotiations with General Walter Gleiniger. In October 2026, the 143-year-old city hall, the Hôtel de Ville , was set on fire by rioters during the 2026 French student protests . The building was largely destroyed. [ 12 ] Climate [ edit ] Limoges experiences an oceanic climate ( Köppen climate classification : Cfb ) common to much of Western France. Most precipitation occurs between October and February. On 27 December 1999, winds reached 148 km/h (92 mph) . On average, the city experiences 41 days of frost and 18 days of snow each winter. In June, July and August, precipitation tends to come only from violent thunderstorms coming from the Bay of Biscay . [ 18 ] It was discovered in the 1960s while building an underground parking lot (place de la république). Remains of the Gallo-Roman amphitheatre, one of the largest in ancient Gaul. [ citation needed ] The Gothic Limoges Cathedral (Cathédrale Saint-Étienne de Limoges), begun in 1273 and only finished in 1888. It is noted for a fine loft built in 1534 and for the partly octagonal bell tower. The main artistic works are a Renaissance rood screen and the tomb of the bishop Jean de Langeac, with sculpted scenes of the Apocalypse. The Chapelle Saint-Aurélien (14th–17th centuries). It includes the relics of St. Aurelian , the second bishop of Limoges , and has medieval statues and Baroque works of art. The church of St-Pierre-du-Queyroix , begun in the 12th century The Church of St-Michel-des-Lions , begun in 1364. It houses the relics of St. Martial and has stained-glass windows from the 15th–16th century. The most striking feature is the 65 m-high tower, with a spire surmounted by a big bronze ball. The bridges of Saint Martial (dating from the Roman era) and of St-Étienne (13th century). The Limoges Fine Arts Museum (Musée des Beaux-Arts), housed in the 18th-century bishops' palace ('Palais de l'Évêché'). [ 19 ] The Hôtel de Ville , completed in 1883, bell tower and roof burnt down on 17 October 2026. [ 20 ] The railway station, Gare de Limoges Bénédictins , inaugurated in 1929. The Château de La Borie (17th century), 4 km (2.5 mi) from the city. It is home to the Centre Culturel de Rencontre de La Borie et l'Ensemble Baroque de Limoges. The remains of the 12th-century Castle of Chalucet, 10 km (6.2 mi) south of the city. During the Hundred Years' War it was a base of bands of pillagers who ravaged the country. The city's botanical gardens include the Jardin botanique de l'Evêché next to the cathedral. The University of Limoges was founded in 1968. [ 21 ] Art and literature [ edit ] The murder of Thomas Becket , Limoges enamel , 12th century, Louvre Museum "Le marché de Limoges" (Limoges market) is the name of a section of Pictures at an Exhibition by Modest Mussorgsky . In 1768, [ 10 ] kaolin , a rock rich in fine, white clay which is used for making porcelain , was discovered at Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche , 30 km south of Limoges. Under the impetus of the progressive economist Anne Robert Jacques Turgot, Baron de Laune , who had been appointed intendant of this impoverished and isolated region, a new ceramics industry was developed, and Limoges porcelain became famous during the 19th century. However, Limoges porcelain is a generic term for porcelain produced in Limoges rather than at a specific factory (there are still several porcelain factories in and around Limoges). More than 50% of all porcelain made in France comes from Limoges. [ 10 ] Education [ edit ] Limoges hosts the national ceramics school École d'ingénieurs ENSIL-ENSCI , created in 1893, [ 22 ] and also the University of Limoges . Sports [ edit ] The city is one of France's basketball capitals. The Palais des Sports de Beaublanc , has been host for international basketball events such as the EuroBasket 1983 and serves as home court for the professional team CSP Limoges (Cercle St Pierre). Since 1983, the club has been French champion 11 times (1983, 1984, 1985, 1988, 1989, 1990, 1993, 1994, 2000, 2014, 2015) and 5 European titles (1982, 1983, 2000 ( Korac Cup ), 1988 (FIBA Saporta Cup), 1993 (Euroleague)). It was the first French club team to become European champion in a collective sport. [ 23 ] [ 24 ] The team currently plays in Pro A , the French first basketball professional league. The city's main stadium is the Beaublanc Stadium . [ 25 ] Limoges Hand 87 is a French handball team based in Limoges, France, which is currently playing in the Division 2 of Ligue Nationale de Handball. Limoges FC was the major city association football team before the club folded in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic . Their home games were played at Stade St. Lazare. USA Limoges is an amateur rugby union club, based in Limoges. Currently competing in Fédérale 1, the top level of the French amateur rugby pyramid and one level below the professional leagues. Transport [ edit ] The main railway station of Limoges is the Limoges-Bénédictins station . It offers direct connections with Paris , and Toulouse, and several regional destinations. Limoges was the last major urban centre of Metropolitan France to be connected to the national motorway system; since the early 1990s, the motorway A20 has connected Limoges with Châteauroux , Vierzon , Orléans and Paris to the north, and Brive-la-Gaillarde , Cahors , Montauban and Toulouse to the south. The nearest airport is Limoges – Bellegarde Airport . Urban transport in Limoges and its metropolitan area is operated by Société de transports en commun de Limoges Métropole (STCL). The Limoges urban bus network includes the Limoges trolleybus system , one of only four such systems currently operating in France. [ 7 ] Demonstrations and protests against poor school and economic conditions by lycée (high school) students have taken place in France since September 2026. In early October, the protests developed into a nationwide mobilisation involving students, teachers, parents, political organizations and trade unions , with an estimated 550,000–800,000 people participating nationwide. [ 8 ] [ 9 ] The demonstrations are part of a wider European unrest which includes protests in Belgium, [ 10 ] [ 11 ] Albania , Greece, [ 12 ] Italy , [ 13 ] [ 14 ] Portugal , Spain , Austria, Ireland, Serbia and Germany. [ 15 ] [ 16 ] The movement is marked by demonstrations and high school blockades. Explaining the protests, students have cited teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and limited public investment in social programs and infrastructure. [ 17 ] [ 18 ] [ 19 ] Students noted stress linked to the university application website Parcoursup [ 18 ] [ 19 ] and high temperatures in classrooms that reached up to 40 °C (104 °F) during the 2026 European heatwaves . [ 20 ] Protesters in France and across Europe complained of high inflation, rents, fuel costs, and unemployment, coupled with social spending cuts. [ 15 ] The initial police response used a variety of forceful crowd-control weapons, resulting in serious injuries, including to children, and violent conflict between police and protestors have led to 6,800 arrests, most of them of minors. [ 21 ] [ 22 ] [ 23 ] [ 24 ] [ 25 ] The French government has accused the far-left of stirring up the unrest for political gain. [ 26 ] [ 27 ] Protesters said the movement was spontaneous and accused the government and right-wing parties of conspiratorial thinking. [ 28 ] The police response drew criticism from human rights organisations: Amnesty International denounced a "disproportionate" use of force, [ 22 ] Human Rights Watch reported serious injuries to children, [ 21 ] and the UN Human Rights Office expressed concern, "[calling] on everyone to ensure that the protests in France remained peaceful and that there is no disproportionate use of force". [ 29 ] The government rejected accusations of police repression, with Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez maintaining that the response had been proportionate in almost all cases and that some protests had turned into riots. [ 30 ] Background Study conditions and government budget The protests came at the start of the school year and at the same time as a public-sector strike over the government's budget plans, which include €61 billion in new spending cuts. [ 17 ] [ 31 ] Students cited unfilled teaching posts, overcrowded classes, long timetables and deteriorating facilities among their grievances. [ 18 ] A 17-year-old pupil at the Lycée Paul-Éluard in Saint-Denis described temporary toilets without water, rats and cockroaches in school, and temperatures ranging from −5 °C in winter to 40 °C in summer in temporary classrooms. [ 32 ] Another pupil described rooms with too few tables, noting that teachers had explained their own discontent before the pupils decided to join them. [ 19 ] Ryad Rani, president of the secondary-students' union Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), cited a pupil who had gone seven months without a French teacher in a year with a French exam, and classes of 32 to 36 students. [ 33 ] Pupils elsewhere told ICI of classes of 35. [ 25 ] High fuel costs, rents, general inflation, unemployment, and government spending cuts have motivated protestors both in France and across Europe. [ 132 ] At the Athénée Paul-Brusson in Montegnée , RTBF reported a quiet blockade in support of teachers, with no clash. [ 129 ] [ 133 ] [ 134 ] [ 11 ] A fire near Brussels-Central railway station on 9 October during student protests By 5 October, protests spread to other major cities in Wallonia such as Mons and Charleroi , as well as the Brussels-Capital Region . In Charleroi, 21 student protesters were arrested on 5 October who set fire to dumpsters using electric scooter batteries. [ 135 ] Blockades were put before Athénée Charles Janssens in the Brussels municipality of Ixelles . [ 136 ] On 6 October, The New York Times reported that protests had spread to high schools in Belgium, where police dispersed peaceful protestors. Police spokesperson Jadranka Lozina accused students of vandalism. [ 137 ] On 7 October, riots gripped Liège, following earlier student protests, prompting authorities to close Liège-Guillemins railway station and urging local businesses to shut down. [ 138 ] Albania See also: Flamingo Revolution and 2026 Albanian student protests Starting on 13 October in Tirana , students rioted and set fires, including attacking the government building of the Ministry of Education . The situation escalated, with riot police being involved. RENEA units were deployed on the 17th. The protests were ongoing as of 22 October. [ 139 ] [ 140 ] [ 141 ] Argentina On 15 October, students protested in Buenos Aires to decry President Javier Milei 's budget cuts to education. [ 142 ] The protest followed a similar incident in May, where an estimated 1.5 million protested nationwide on 15 October. [ 143 ] [ 144 ] According to the Center for National Economic Research at the University of Buenos Aires, at the University of Buenos Aires, real public spending on universities fell by 41% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, amid a dispute over the government's implementation of the University Funding Law. [ 145 ] Italy Main article: 2026 Italian unrest This section is an excerpt from 2026 European unrest § Italy . [ edit ] A broken shopfront in Milan , Lombardy , after the riots On 16 October, Italian students in major cities like Milan , Turin , Bologna , Genoa , Verona , Rome , and Bari started protesting, inspired by their French counterparts. The mobilization was denominated No Meloni Day , referring to Giorgia Meloni , the Prime Minister of Italy . Demonstrators protested against the conditions of Italian educational facilities, against the measures adopted by the government to limit the number of foreign students in classrooms, [ 146 ] and demanded that the government start spending more on education and less on weapons. [ 147 ] [ 148 ] [ 149 ] In Rome, demonstrators threw firecrackers and cherry bombs in front of the Ministry of Education, calling for Giuseppe Valditara , the Italian Minister of Education, and asking him to "get out of the building". During the second day of the protest, 17 October, in Milan, Turin, and Bologna, small riots split off from the protests, which had developed to encompass general social and economic discontent. Milan saw increased cases of rioting, with many luxury storefronts reported looted. [ 150 ] [ 151 ] The students' protest became part of a broader climate of social protest. The movement saw road haulers and farmers joining the protests and going on strike because of the high cost of diesel fuel and the rising of the already high cost of living. Severe fuel shortages were reported in Southern Italy, alongside empty shelves in supermarkets. [ 152 ] [ 153 ] [ 154 ] [ 155 ] In Apulia , students, road haulers, and farmers demonstrated together. Minister of Infrastructure and Transport Matteo Salvini scheduled a meeting with representatives of road haulers for 20 October in Milan. Representatives of Calabrian road haulers have said that they won't stop striking and demonstrating if the confrontation with the government does not result in a satisfying outcome. [ 156 ] Greece On 13 October, Greek students began protests in the Syntagma Square of Athens , which are centered around the issues of unaffordable prices of living for students, mainly in terms of student housing. Additionally protestors brought up complaints of the lack of funding for the public education system. Demonstrators erected tents outside of the Ministry of National Economy and Finance and the Hellenic Parliament , mainly as a blockade, but according to the Hellenic Broadcasting Corporation the tents are also a comment about the condition of housing in Greece. [ 12 ] [ 157 ] The organizers said that the tents were planned to stand for the following two days, and then a protest concert would be held the following week on 20 October. [ 158 ] [ 159 ] Canada On 17 October, a protest in solidarity with the students in France was held in Montreal , focusing on rising cost of living and police misconduct. [ 160 ] [ 161 ] Other Smaller protests have occurred in Austria, Ireland, Portugal, and Germany. [ 16 ] [ 15 ] Incidents Paris and Seine-Saint-Denis Police firing tear gas during clashes at Porte Saint-Martin in Paris, 17 October In Saint-Denis, the Lycée Paul-Éluard was closed after fires at the gates. CNN reported that fencing was torn down. [ 32 ] Le Figaro reported soot on the bitumen, fire damage on the metal gates, and banners denouncing lack of resources and police violence. It said the Lycée Frédéric Bartholdi was also closed, that courses were cancelled, and that a handful of students from Paris 8 and Paris 13 remained after the lycée pupils had left. [ 162 ] On 28 September, HuffPost reported clashes at the same lycée, with tear gas used against pupils, arrests, fireworks and other projectiles thrown at police. [ 163 ] On 29 September, Paris Match reported bins set on fire in front of the gates, a call to the fire service, and two arrests at about 8:15 a.m. [ 164 ] A CLPRESS video from the same morning showed a fence falling after pupils shook it. [ 165 ] RMC reported that the principal of the Lycée Jean-Pierre-Timbaud in Aubervilliers was slightly burned by a firework, and that a principal in Val-de-Marne was grazed by a firework and shocked but not injured. [ 166 ] On 17 October, a 17-year-old pupil had his right hand blown off with a crowd-control grenade in Saint-Etienne. [ 167 ] In Pantin , BFM reported a fire lit in front of the Lycée Berthelot and fireworks fired at the pupils. [ 168 ] The Île-de-France regional authority said more than 200 lycées were disrupted, about 50 of them the scene of violence, and that about 30 gates or entrance locks had been damaged, at a cost it put above €1 million. [ 46 ] [ 169 ] On 28 September in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône , Val-d'Oise , a 14-year-old's lawyer, Elsa Marcel , said he had a double jaw fracture, broken upper teeth and several broken lower teeth, and that he required heavy surgery. [ 170 ] [ 65 ] [ 171 ] The Défenseur des droits opened an inquiry. Nuñez said the IGPN had been asked to investigate injuries to lycée students in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, Sevran , and Tours. [ 65 ] Firefighters extinguish a burning car during riots in Paris, 17 October In Paris, the prefecture of police said a young policewoman who had stopped to pick up a fallen radio was caught by several people, and kicked. The assault was filmed. She filed a complaint. The prefect said the acts were unspeakable. [ 172 ] Europe 1 reported that Ritchy Thibault [ fr ] , 23, a former parliamentary assistant to LFI deputy Ersilia Soudais, was arrested in Saint-Denis on 1 October during the blockades. On a video filmed by a participant, he told the crowd that 17 October would be "a thousand times worse than the Yellow Vests", and then: "We're going to build barricades. We're going to set fire to the Élysée. We're going to make the Revolution." Europe 1 said he was under judicial supervision that barred him from demonstrations, and that he was listed as a security threat. [ 173 ] Hauts-de-France On 30 September in Roubaix , ICI reported that the entrance door of the private Lycée Léonard-de-Vinci caught fire after bins were set alight. A pupil who passed at about 7:30 a.m. put the crowd at least 200. Firefighters and police attended, and tear gas was used. The school cancelled classes for Wednesday and Thursday. [ 174 ] La Voix du Nord reported gatherings that morning at Saint-Martin, Léonard-de-Vinci, and Saint-Rémi, with bin fires that damaged a door and a gate. It said about 100 teenagers then marched to Jean-Moulin, where the entrance grilles were taken down, and that police pushed back about 150 pupils at Baudelaire. At Louis-Loucheur, bins were burned and people tried to pull the gate off. The Nord prefecture told ICI that 29 schools in the department were disrupted that day and that 25 people were arrested. [ 175 ] In Lille on 1 October, Ouest-France reported burning bins and projectiles thrown at riot police near the neighbouring lycées Gaston-Berger and Faidherbe, and police charges with tear gas. franceinfo reported a police intervention at Faidherbe. [ 66 ] La Voix du Nord reported that Tuesday's mobilisation included serious damage at the Lycée César-Baggio, where a teacher was assaulted. [ 176 ] ICI reported bins burned and bus shelters smashed at Baggio on 29 September, with tear gas used against a crowd of about 200. [ 177 ] [ 178 ] In Haubourdin , near Lille, franceinfo reported that municipal buildings were ransacked, that the Lycée Beaupré stayed closed on Thursday and Friday, and that two nearby schools were also closed. [ 66 ] ICI reported bins burned there and wrote that the lycée and the two nearby schools would stay closed until Monday. [ 179 ] On 28 September, La Voix du Nord reported that about 100 young people burned tires and pieces of wood outside Beaupré, and that police used tear gas. [ 180 ] [ 181 ] In Tourcoing , La Voix du Nord reported that at the Lycée Sévigné a young man was found unconscious on the ground and got up a few minutes later. After police arrived, the crowd scattered. Some people arrived with sticks and fire extinguishers, and projectiles including glass bottles and stones were thrown at police. Police used tear gas and fired rubber-bullet rounds. [ 182 ] In Auchel , Pas-de-Calais , the principal of the vocational lycée Fernand-Degrugillier was hit by a projectile and hospitalised, the prefecture told ICI. [ 66 ] [ 25 ] BFM Grand Lille, citing the sub-prefect of Béthune and the prefecture, reported that the projectile was a firework that struck him in the ear, and that the rectorat would file a complaint. [ 183 ] RMC, citing the Béthune prosecutor, reported a lit firecracker that bounced and exploded about two metres from him. [ 166 ] La Voix du Nord reported that an 18-year-old girl was burned on the neck by an aerosol used to feed a bin fire at the Lycée Léo-Lagrange in Bully-les-Mines , and that a 15-year-old girl in Arras was hospitalised with a scalp wound after being hit by a projectile. [ 182 ] Normandy The Normandy rectorat said the principals of the Lycée Blaise-Pascal in Rouen and the Lycée Élisa-Lemonnier in Le Petit-Quevilly were assaulted and slightly injured. [ 184 ] [ 185 ] Tendance Ouest, citing the academy, reported that the Blaise-Pascal principal was targeted by a firework, hit in the abdomen, and burned, and that he stayed on site. [ 186 ] Paris-Normandie reported that a fire of bins, pallets, and other objects heavily damaged the doors and entrances of Blaise-Pascal, and that the building itself did not catch fire. It said the principal was injured by a firework that morning, and that the school, already blockaded on 30 September, would stay closed until 5 October. [ 187 ] actu.fr reported five people injured across the academy, material damage inside some blockaded lycées, 33 fire-service callouts, and more than 240 firefighters. It placed bin fires at the gates of Blaise-Pascal, not inside the building, and also at Marcel-Sembat in Sotteville-lès-Rouen and at Camille-Saint-Saëns in central Rouen. [ 185 ] ICI separately reported a fire at Blaise-Pascal. [ 25 ] BBC News reported a school entrance on fire in Rouen. [ 24 ] Paris-Normandie reported that a masked group arrived at Marcel-Sembat in Sotteville-lès-Rouen at about 7:45 a.m. with two rows of shopping carts used as barricades, one at the gates and one on rue Léon-Salva. [ 188 ] The rectorat said about 30 lycées in Seine-Maritime would stay closed on 2 October. [ 185 ] In Le Havre , Paris-Normandie reported a large fire of bins and branches outside the Lycée Porte-Océane, a heavy police presence, and at least one arrest. It reported several hundred pupils outside Claude-Monet, electric scooters on fire near François-Ier, and a charge toward police that the police answered. [ 189 ] ICI reported fire damage at Porte-Océane, a street fire outside Françoise-de-Grâce, destroyed bins and at least two burned cars near Jules-Siegfried, and a fire at Saint-Vincent-de-Paul. [ 190 ] In Caen , Ouest-France reported barricades at the lycées Malherbe, Rostan

text: 2026 Ethiopian offensive - Wikipedia Jump to content Search Search 2026 Ethiopian offensive 9 languages العربية Беларуская Español فارسی Français Bahasa Indonesia 한국어 Português Русский Edit links From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia For the clashes in the Tigray region earlier this year, see Tigray clashes (January–February 2026) . 2026 Ethiopian offensive Part of Ethiopian civil conflict (2018–present) Controlled by Ethiopia ( ENDF and allied militias) Controlled by the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF) and Eritrean Defense Forces (EDF) Controlled by the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) Controlled by the Fano (Amhara Militia) Controlled by the Afar National Unity Revolutionary Front (ANURF) (For an up-to-date, interactive, detailed map, see here .) Date 23 September 2026 – present (1 month and 2 days) Location Ethiopia and Eritrea Status Ongoing Territorial changes Alliance forces seize Aksum and Shire airports [ 1 ] [ 2 ] TPLF/Afar forces advance in Afar [ 3 ] ENDF advance in southern Tigray 2026 Eritrean incursion into Ethiopia Belligerents Ethiopia Tigray Peace and Change Council Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Coalition for Survival Eritrea [ 4 ] Commanders and leaders Abiy Ahmed Birhanu Jula Getachew Reda Debretsion Gebremichael Zemene Kassie [ 5 ] Ibrahim Osman Aliyu Isaias Afwerki Filipos Woldeyohannes Units involved Federal government ENDF Ethiopian Air Force Ethiopian Army Ethiopian Federal Police Amhara riot police Tigray Peace Force Local militias Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Coalition for Survival TPLF Tigray Defense Forces Fano Amhara Fano National Movement Afar National Unity Revolutionary Front EDF Eritrean Army Casualties and losses Per Fano: 10 military trucks captured [ 6 ] 2 military trucks destroyed [ 7 ] Fano : Several casualties [ 8 ] Per Ethiopia: 272 killed, 260 wounded [ 9 ] v t e Post-1960 conflicts in the Horn of Africa Eritrean War of Independence Eritrean civil wars 1961 revolt in Somalia Bale revolt Ethiopian–Somali conflict 1963 Ogaden Rebellion 1964 Ogaden 1982 Oromo conflict Ethiopian Civil War Somali Civil War Rebellion Puntland–Somaliland 2006–09 2009–present Somaliland War of Independence Djiboutian Civil War Insurgency in Ogaden Second Afar insurgency Eritrean–Ethiopian War OEF – Horn of Africa Djiboutian–Eritrean conflict Ethiopian civil conflict Oromia Benishangul-Gumuz Tigray Amhara Northern Ethiopia On 23 September 2026, the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Coalition for Survival , a coalition of various Ethiopian rebel and insurgent groups, launched a large-scale military offensive against the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) in Tigray , Afar and Amhara . [ 10 ] The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) described the offensive as a defensive war against the federal government of Ethiopia . [ 11 ] [ 12 ] [ 13 ] The TPLF took control of several towns bordering Tigray Region. Control shifted back to federal forces, with the ENDF retaking control of Afar towns and capturing the Tigray capital Mekelle . Eritrean troops entered Tigray while the ENDF continued advancing north in Tigray Region. The offensive was the largest escalation in fighting since the Tigray war (2020 – 2022), which was one of the bloodiest conflicts of the 21st century . [ 14 ] Background Tigray war and Pretoria agreement Further information: Tigrayan peace process , Ethiopia–Tigray peace agreement , and Reinstatement of the Tigray Regional Council The TPLF was effectively the ruling party of Ethiopia, dominating the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) from 1991 to 2018. In 2018, Abiy Ahmed was elected leader of the EPRDF and thus became prime minister. The Tigray war took place under Abiy's leadership from November 2020 to November 2022, when Ethiopia and the TPLF signed the Pretoria agreement . [ 15 ] The situation remained unstable, with officials from the Amhara Region continuing to occupy Western Tigray and the government launching a series of drone strikes in 2025 while the TPLF amassed troops at the border. [ 16 ] [ 17 ] [ 18 ] In May 2025, the National Election Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) revoked the TPLF's registration as a political party, despite the TPLF being a signatory, alongside the federal government, to the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement that ended the Tigray War. [ 19 ] In response, the TPLF declared the restoration of the pre-war administration and installed the TPLF's chairman Debretsion Gebremichael [ 13 ] as Tigray's regional president, creating a rival government to that of the pro-government Interim Regional Administration of Tigray . [ 20 ] [ 21 ] [ 22 ] 2026 clashes and escalation In late January and early February 2026, days-long clashes erupted in Tigray between the TPLF and the ENDF, in what Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) described as the most significant fighting between the two since full-scale war. [ 23 ] Relations between the central government and TPLF continued to deteriorate, and by mid-July the TPLF declared the Pretoria agreement "effectively dead". [ 24 ] On 1 August, a battle lasting several hours broke out between the ENDF and the TPLF near the Sudan border. [ 24 ] [ 25 ] In subsequent weeks, the ENDF carried out numerous drone strikes in Tigray. [ 26 ] [ 27 ] The regional capital of Mekelle was hit by a series of drone strikes in late August, including an attack on 20 August against a residential compound with no obvious military targets that wounded 13 civilians. [ 28 ] Prelude Declaration of the Ethiopian People's Forces Coalition for Survival Main article: Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Coalition for Survival Logo for EPFAS On 20 September 2026, the formal declaration of an alliance of Ethiopian rebel groups from Tigray and the Somali Region , named the Ethiopian People's Forces Coalition for Survival (EPFAS) — alternatively "Tsimdo" or the "Alliance for Survival" — was announced. [ 29 ] [ 30 ] [ 31 ] Reported to contain between 6 and 8 [ clarification needed ] members, the coalition was declared to comprise the: Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) [ 9 ] Tigray Defense Forces / Tigray People's Liberation Front (TDF/TPLF) [ 9 ] Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) [ 9 ] Ogaden National Liberation Front (denied by Qalbidhagax-led faction, ONLF) [ a ] [ 9 ] Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (per Al Jazeera English and Critical Threats Project , ARDUF/Ugugumo) [ 33 ] [ 9 ] or the Afar National Unity Revolutionary Front (per Addis Standard and Al Jazeera English, ANURF) [ 34 ] [ 35 ] Benishangul People's Liberation Front/ Benishangul People's Liberation Movement (BPLF/BPLM) Gumuz People's Democratic Movement (denied, GPDM). [ 33 ] [ 9 ] The coalition, consisting of some members which fought against each other during the 2020–2022 Tigray war, [ 30 ] pledged to overthrow the Abiy Ahmed -led government towards establishing a transitional government . [ 33 ] On 26 September, GPDM denied membership of the coalition, claiming it had no military apparatus. [ 36 ] The Abdirahman Mohamed Sheikh Mahdi-led ONLF faction asserted ONLF membership of the coalition, which the Jijiga -based ONLF faction led by Abdikarin Sheikh Muse Qalbidhagax denied. [ 37 ] [ 38 ] Offensive 22–28 September 2026: Early EPFAS gains repelled thereafter by ENDF counteroffensive For a chronological guide, see Timeline of the 2026 Ethiopian offensive . Primary points of fighting between 22 and 28 September, including airport seizures Regions: Afar , Tigray , Amhara On 22 September 2026, the ENDF launched drone attacks on EPFAS positions, including on a school in Alamata which killed 14 civilians and injured 22 more [ 39 ] [ 40 ] — hostilities which the TDF/TPLF labelled an "open invasion" before claiming it would respond with a "defensive war." [ 9 ] [ 41 ] The following morning, 23 September, the EPFAS — primarily including TDF/TPLF fighters [ 31 ] — launched an offensive on government positions first along the Kobo –Tumuga front, [ 42 ] then along the border of the Afar and Amhara regions. [ 31 ] [ 9 ] [ 36 ] They additionally seized the airports of Axum , Shire , and Mekelle ( Alula Aba Nega Airport ) — which are all located in northern Tigray; [ 31 ] [ 9 ] [ 10 ] [ 20 ] [ 43 ] the captures and halting of flight services cut the ENDP's only means of sending reinforcements directly into the Tigray region. [ 9 ] This initial offensive was relatively successful initially, capturing Abala and the Erebti District on 22 and 27 September, respectively. [ 9 ] [ 44 ] Successful attacks would also reach down into northeastern Amhara Region. [ 9 ] [ 36 ] The ENDF halted EPFAS approaches towards the Amhara Region's North Wollo Zone capital town of Weldiya , [ 9 ] [ 44 ] [ 45 ] moving troops north along the A2 highway connecting Weldiya to Mekelle — the axis along which most of the fighting had taken place. [ 9 ] [ 44 ] [ 46 ] The rebels did make some advances, EPFAS forces opened another front in the Wag Hemra Zone , in western Amhara region — on 24 September, which was largely under government control. [ 9 ] This movement marked an ENDF success on the eastern front, which was replicated in the west, [ 44 ] where the ENDF repelled forces from the Amhara to the Tigray Region, having recaptured the town of Soqota on 27 September. [ 47 ] Furthermore, they succeeded in containing battles along the Tigray border. This was illustrated by the fact that hostilities continued in Abala, Mekelle, and Lalibela [ 48 ] [ 11 ] while new fighting broke out only in the northeast of the North Wollo Zone. [ 36 ] [ 45 ] The ENDF soon launched a counter offensive and began entering Tigray , with pro-government forces capturing Alamata on 28 September, [ 49 ] [ 50 ] during which at least 52 civilians were killed. [ 51 ] 29 September–11 October 2026: Addis Ababa strikes, Eritrean troops and continued hostilities For a chronological guide, see Timeline of the 2026 Ethiopian offensive . Further information: 2026 Eritrean incursion into Ethiopia and Eritrea–Ethiopia relations § Tigray War and new hostilities Towns and cities like Mekelle, including the civilian victims therein, were also targets during the Tigray war Despite accusations by the Ethiopian government of Eritrea's financial and diplomatic collaboration with rebels, [ 30 ] [ 52 ] Eritrean officials denied involvement in the formation of the coalition. [ 53 ] Ethiopian officials accused Eritrea of troop presence in northern Ethiopia beginning on 29 September. [ 54 ] [ 55 ] ACLED and witnesses speaking to Reuters and The Guardian reported Eritrean troops entering Tigray on 7 October. [ 56 ] [ 57 ] However, ties between Eritrea and Ethiopia broke down before this confirmation, when on 1 October, deep-penetration drone attacks orchestrated by EPFAS exploded in Addis Ababa, primarily targeting military air facilities. [ 44 ] [ 15 ] The attacks served to stretch ENDF resources and displace focus away from the primary theaters of battle near Tigray Region. [ 44 ] In response, the Ethiopian foreign ministry closed its embassy in Asmara after accusing Eritrea of "direct and indirect hostility," causing the de facto breaking of diplomatic ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea. [ 58 ] [ 59 ] [ 60 ] ENDF forces continued to approach Mekelle through the A2 highway, with hostilities beginning near the road — between Korem and Maychew . [ 44 ] By 30 September, the ENDF had reportedly captured Abala, Korem, and other positions along the A2. [ 44 ] On the eastern front, the ENDF secured control of Abala and Erebti by 1 October. [ 36 ] The recapture precluded an EPFAS advance to sever the A1 highway to Djibouti , whose port handles 90% of Ethiopian imports and exports. [ 44 ] EPFAS withdrew forces positioned along the A1 to defend the A2 and Mekelle [ 44 ] — with a pro-government militia commander and Horn Review stating that the rebel forces would soon be reinforced by Eritrean troops arriving through the Assab – Bure front to the border Afar towns of Berhale and Dallol , reaching up to 20 km (12 mi) away from Adigrat . [ 61 ] [ 62 ] Between 3 and 4 October, the ENDF recaptured Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle and surrounded the city before EPFAS troops abandoned it. [ 2 ] [ 63 ] [ 64 ] Following ENDF mobilizations along the Eritrean border following the EPFAS retreat from Adigrat on 5 October, [ 65 ] the ENDF attacked EDF troops traveling towards Idaga Hamus with drones. The EDF arrived in Idaga Hamus on 7 October. [ 4 ] [ 66 ] ENDF troops occupied Agula , previously occupied by the TPLF. [ 67 ] The following day, on 8 October, more Eritrean troops were seen arriving, [ 68 ] having passed through Zalambessa . [ 67 ] The ENDF attacked EDF troops with drones on both 7 and 8 October. [ 69 ] The ENDF captured Wukro , crossed the Tekezé River and occupied Adi Gebru . [ 67 ] [ 68 ] Attacks on Eritrean forces' positions caused them, according to a witness speaking with Agence France-Presse (AFP), to retreat north following ENDF attacks on 9 October. [ 69 ] The following day, on 10 October, the ENDF regained control of Adigrat. [ 70 ] A witness told Agence France-Presse that Eritrean forces appeared to retreat north following ENDF attacks. [ 69 ] On 9 October, Fano forces captured Anchekorer . [ citation needed ] On 10 October the ENDF regained control of Adigrat. [ 70 ] The EDF held positions north of Adigrat. [ 71 ] On 11 October, ENDF and TPF took control of Adwa . [ 71 ] [ 72 ] An Ethiopian government source told UMD Media that on 11 October the ENDF occupied the Eritrean border village of Deba Sima in the Southern Denkalya subregion , 50 kilometres (31 mi) from Assab. [ 73 ] Afar locals speaking to UMD Media disputed that the ENDF had done so. [ 74 ] On 14 October, Fano claimed to have captured the town of Meragna in Amhara's North Shewa Zone . [ 75 ] [ 76 ] 12 October 2026–present: continued ENDF advance ENDF troops took control of Zalambessa on 12 October. EPFAS troops had left earlier. [ 71 ] [ 77 ] EPFAS troops took control of Fatsi, Adi Daero , Adi Nbried, Adi Hageray, and Adi Awala. [ 71 ] The UN Security Council (UNSC) held a closed-door meeting on the situation in the Horn of Africa . [ 77 ] The Security Council Report (SCR) argued that UNSC members seemed "increasingly concerned about the interstate dimension of the recent escalation". [ 78 ] On 16 October, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed announced the formation of a new interim government for the Tigray Region intended to operate for six months before holding elections. [ 79 ] [ 80 ] Four chief executives were appointed, with the President of the Executive Committee position expected to rotate between the four. [ 81 ] Most of the officials appointed to the interim government had previously split from the TPLF. [ 82 ] Peace process See also: Ethiopia–Tigray peace agreement and Tigrayan peace process The takeover of the three Tigray Region airports by Tigrayan forces was a violation of the Pretoria Agreement according to the African Union (AU) Commission (AUC) chairperson , Mahamoud Ali Youssouf . On 23 September 2026, Youssouf requested Olusegun Obasanjo , African Union High Representative for the Horn of Africa, to carry out negotiations to preserve the peace process. [ 83 ] On 2 October, Amnesty International called for the AU Peace and Security Council to hold an emergency session, arguing that the AU "was one of the guarantors" of the Pretoria Agreement. [ 84 ] Consequences Withdrawal from Somalia Further information: Ethiopian–Somali conflict § AMISOM/ATMIS/AUSSOM and non-AU Ethiopian forces (2014 – present) Bloomberg reported that Ethiopia plans to withdraw 3,000 soldiers from Somalia. Somalia said it had been not informed of such plans. It was not immediately known whether or how a withdrawal would impact the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia or other, bilateral deployments. [ 85 ] [ 86 ] [ 87 ] Diplomatic crisis with Eritrea Main article: Eritrea–Ethiopia relations On 1 October 2026, the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced it was shutting its embassy in Asmara due to the alleged Eritrean involvement in the conflict and expelled 10 diplomats ordering them to leave the country within 48 hours and declaring them as persona non grata . [ 88 ] [ 89 ] In response, Eritrea announced the severance of all diplomatic ties with its Ministry of Foreign Affairs saying on X that it, "had no choice but to reciprocate". [ 90 ] [ 89 ] Eritrea stated that one of its fears was that Ethiopia would utilize the conflict to initiate an offensive on the port of Assab , [ 91 ] and added that Ethiopia's latest escalations signified a "publicly pronounced declaration of war " and an attempt at regime change . [ 92 ] On 5 October, Abiy was sworn in for another term as Prime Minister of Ethiopia, and in a speech immediately after he stated that he would "work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea". [ 93 ] Humanitarian crisis Food insecurity and famine Main article: Famine in northern Ethiopia (2020–present) Further information: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification § Ethiopia Beginning with the onset of the Tigray war in November 2020, acute food shortages leading to death and starvation became widespread in northern Ethiopia, and the Tigray, Afar and Amhara Regions in particular. While the situation improved after the March 2022 truce and allowed for humanitarian distribution of food, the lack of rain in the spring of 2022 compounded the already existing food insecurity. [ 94 ] The resurgence of fighting after the ceasefire collapsed in August 2022 exacerbated the situation even more; by October, between 400 and 900 a day were dying of starvation. [ 95 ] As of October 2026, areas in the southern Tigray were facing droughts which prolonged food insecurity into "crisis-level conditions" as classified by Phase 3 of the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). Fighting disrupted fuel supplies, market activity, transportation, harvests — physically and monetarily restricting access to food, farmland, labor opportunities, and other essential goods. According to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET), these conditions risked the IPC Phase 3 conditions continuing. [ 96 ] Internet and telephone access Due to the intense fighting in Northern Ethiopia, the internet connection in the area was disrupted, alongside telephone lines, which prevented news agencies and families from contacting external regions and individuals within the region itself. [ 97 ] War crimes See also: War crimes in the Tigray war According to Human Rights Watch (HRW), the ENDF 20 August strike against the Daero area of Mekelle , during the leadup to the September conflict, was "unlawfully indiscriminate" since it had "no evident military targets". HRW's evidence included interviews with three survivors, two medical workers, and two residents, and analysis of photographic, video, and satellite evidence. The 20 August attack was the dropping of a bomb by an aircraft on a residential compound for teachers around 11:00 local time. A 4 m (13 ft) diameter crater resulted from the bombing. [ 28 ] HRW recommended investigation into the 20 August Daero attack as a possible war crime . [ 28 ] Witnesses speaking to The Guardian reported a campaign of forced recruitment by rebels in Tigray, including the conscription at gunpoint of children as young as 15. [ 98 ] Reactions Governments Australia : The Department of Foreign Affairs advised its citizens against unnecessary travel to Ethiopia, and issued a Do Not Travel warning to the conflict areas. [ 99 ] United States : According to Washington Examiner , the United States (US) advised its citizens against traveling to the Tigray and Afar regions and prohibited U.S. government personnel from traveling there. [ 100 ] [ better source needed ] The United States Department of State released a statement urging both Ethiopia and Eritrea to show restraint, citing cross-border "tensions". It argued the latter would require mediation by the AU and Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia , and a long-term port deal for Ethiopia through Assab, Berbera or Djibouti. Ethiopia westerly borders Sudan , which has been entrenched in conflict since 1955 and a civil war since 2023. Two primary belligerents, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), fight along an East – West divide. Ethiopia involved itself in the present conflict in February 2026, when researchers from Reuters conducted a visual investigation revealing Ethiopia's hosting of a training camp for RSF militants, [ 106 ] set along the two countries' border, specifically the Blue Nile State , where the RSF since launched a new front. [ 107 ] [ 108 ] Compounded by accusations of Ethiopian-launched drone strikes into Sudan, the Sudanese government subsequently accused Ethiopia of its involvement in the civil war a month later, in March. [ 109 ] [ 110 ] [ 111 ] Ethiopia's support for the RSF facilitated the RSF's efforts in the southeastern front it launched in January, along Sudan's border with Ethiopia, [ 112 ] including allowing the RSF to launch offensives from Ethiopian territory as reported in August. [ 113 ] Foreign involvement has been a cornerstone of the civil war's intractability , with primary funding of the SAF coming from Saudi Arabia and the RSF from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) [ 114 ] — funding which has been labelled as containing elements of proxy conflict , [ 115 ] extractivism , [ 116 ] and a Saudi Arabian-Emirati rivalry . [ 117 ] [ 118 ] Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed ( left ) and Somaliland President Muse Bihi Abdi ( right ) exchanging the MoU after its signing Ethiopia easterly borders Somalia , which has also entrenched in a civil war since between 1978 and 1991, with the present phase beginning in 2009. It is being fought between the internationally-recognized Somali government's military wing, the Somali National Army (SNA); the Somali Future Council , an opposition coalition; Islamic State (IS)-affiliated groups including al-Shabaab and Somalia Wilayah ; and the self-declared state of Somaliland . On the military front, Al-Shabaab regained much of its territorial losses in the 2022 – 2023 government offensive thanks it part to deepening ties with the Houthis in Yemen [ 119 ] [ 120 ] [ 121 ] — another ongoing conflict being waged across the Bab al-Mandab Strait from the Horn and more recently within it , since September 2026 — risking escalation in the Somali civil war, as further complicated by warnings of the African Union (AU) Support and Stabilization Mission's (AUSSOM) potential collapse following the cessation of US funding beyond December of that year. [ 119 ] [ 122 ] [ 123 ] On the diplomatic front, Ethiopia and Somaliland signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) in January 2024, giving Ethiopia access to the Red Sea through the Port of Berbera in return for its recognition of Somaliland . [ 124 ] [ 125 ] Despite agreeing to restore bilateral relations through the Ankara Declaration — signed in Turkey that following December — through which it restating its recognition of Somalia's sovereign territory, analysts underscored that it created a precarious peace.
